properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
After visiting the flour mill and observing the conservation process carried out there, we had some criticism of some of the actions taken. Firstly, a stone base was added to the roof railing, built in the 1990s. This addition changes the original shape of the mill structure and harms its authenticity. In addition, the roof railings are made of metal, which in our opinion, draws attention and does not connect with the ancient architectural language. Secondly, we would also make the first floor of the mill building usable (it is currently closed) and turn it into an exhibition space that would present the history of the entire site. Finally, we recommend improving and maintaining the viewing window to the grinding mechanism that exists in the mill to illustrate the ancient working methods that were in operation in the past.

Programmatically, we felt a lack in the presentation of the mill's original function. Although the visitor center is located in the flour mill, it does not reflect the values of the building and its original function. The content presented on site and in the film shown is mainly about the reserve and the site in general. We propose designing the interior space as close to the original as possible, so that visitors can learn about the process of flour milling in that period.
(Addition by Yael Alef - it could be interesting to link the mill to the Kurdana mill to illustrate the story of the struggles between the Hospitallers and the Templars) and also to refer to the mound to give historical and spatial context (a dimension of historical depth + a view of the area) to the entire place. It should be noted that the existing route of the reserve's boundaries does not include the mound and the boundary passes adjacent to the mill wall without a buffer zone).
properties.management_data_notes: The name of the approved plan in the Planning Administration is G/2062 Ein Afek Nature Reserve. The Crusader flour mill 'Dok' located in the Ein Afek reserve is under statutory protection as part of the reserve, which was declared an antiquities site and nature reserve in 1979. In 1996, the reserve was recognized as a 'Ramsar site' in accordance with the Ramsar Convention for the conservation and sustainable development of wetlands. The area is declared a conservation site, which ensures its protection and legal enforcement of conservation activities. In terms of management activities, the site is managed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority with daily presence and routine maintenance, including continuous supervision to preserve the values of nature and heritage. In addition, the site is a closed area and entry is conditional on purchasing a ticket.
properties.cultural_assessment_0:
The Crusader flour mill Dok in the Ein Afek reserve is a historical structure with important cultural values, reflecting the heritage of the region and the rich history that existed there over the years. Its location near the Na'aman stream is linked to the importance of the area as an agricultural and industrial center for hundreds of years, and to a large extent, the mill serves as tangible evidence of the Crusader period in the Acre Valley region.

The site has been inhabited since the Canaanite period and throughout history to the present day. The flour mill was built during the 12th century, during the period when the Crusaders ruled the Land of Israel, and was part of a network of flour mills built along the Na'aman stream, utilizing water power to drive large millstones. Among the other flour mills in the area, the Dok mill is the only one from the Crusader period that has remained in good condition. The mill and the entire site are mentioned in Crusader documents, in the context of the struggle between the Hospitaller and Templar orders, and represent the last evidence of the industry that existed on the Na'aman stream from the Crusader period to the British period.

Economically, the mill was a central hub in the development of the region. It provided services to the residents of the nearby villages and the cities that were under Crusader rule, thus contributing significantly to the economic growth of the entire region. Its strategic location on the axis between Acre and Nazareth made it an important factor in the local economic system, as it supplied flour not only for local needs but also for trade with other areas. (Point to be clarified)

The aesthetic value of the flour mill stems from its unique integration into the natural landscape of the Ein Afek reserve, in the heart of the Na'aman stream springs. The structure, built of local kurkar stone, is characterized by thick walls and barrel and cross vaults, reflecting the influence of European medieval architecture on the region. The mill presents a unique combination of Crusader architecture with Ottoman and British influences, expressed in a single structure. The roof offers a panoramic view of the Acre Valley, emphasizing the historical and agricultural importance of the area. The simplicity of the structure and the natural materials from which it was built blend harmoniously with the environment, making the mill an integral part of the landscape. The combination of the stone structure, the flowing water of the Na'aman stream, and the rich vegetation around it creates a unique visual and acoustic experience that connects man and nature.

The state of preservation of the Crusader mill in Ein Afek is relatively good, despite the years that have passed since it was built. The strong walls and massive vaults have withstood the ravages of time, but it is evident that the structure has suffered from cracks and repairs over the years. These repairs were likely made to preserve the structure and continue to use it in the periods after the Crusaders left the area.

The Crusader mill in the Ein Afek reserve is a cultural and historical asset of great value, representing a unique combination of cultural heritage and long-term preservation. The preservation of the mill allows for the preservation of the rich history of the area and the transmission of stories and traditions to future generations. The mill embodies the connection between man and nature, between the past and the present, and is a living testimony to the culture and local heritage of Ein Afek and its surroundings. Therefore, the preservation and research of the site are important not only for understanding the past, but also for preserving our heritage for future generations.

The Crusader structure, with its stone walls and impressive arches, stands as a symbol of the events that took place here hundreds of years ago. Around it, the pastoral landscape of the Afek ponds and marshes, with its calm waters, dense vegetation, and the chirping of birds, enhances the feeling of connection to the land and the people who lived and worked in this place in the past. properties.description:
Geographical-Historical Background:
The Crusader flour mill Dok is located in the Ein Afek Nature Reserve, which is in the northern coastal plain of Israel, in the Zevulun Valley, near Kiryat Bialik and Kiryat Motzkin. The area was formerly a central axis for transportation along the stream and a source of life for agricultural and industrial activity, with the area serving as the agricultural hinterland of Acre during the Crusader period. The mill is located in a place that has been inhabited since the Canaanite period and throughout history to the present day, and has had many uses.
During the Crusader period, the Dok and Rekordana flour mills were established by the Templar and Hospitaller orders, who utilized the Na'aman stream to operate flour mills and transport the products to Acre. The first mill, Rekordana, was built by the Hospitallers, creating a lake by means of a 100-meter-long dam. Later, the Templars built the Dok mill as a fortified structure on Roman-era remains, about 370 meters west of Rekordana, with a large 652-meter-long dam. The proximity between the mills led to conflicts over water regulation and the use of the stream, until the Pope's intervention was required to settle the dispute. During this period, the mill served as a grinding and flour supply mill for the entire Acre Valley and the region, later as a fortress guarding the road from Acre to Nazareth, and during the Sixth Crusade it served as the main headquarters of Emperor Frederick. During the Ottoman period, the mill continued to supply flour to the soldiers stationed there. Later, in addition to being a flour mill, the place served as a distribution center for fish throughout the country. The mill is built as a fortified structure consisting of three adjacent buildings. The mill is built of large stones with diagonal chisel marks typical of the Crusaders, while the Ottoman extension is built of smaller, roughly hewn stones. The ground floor contains five flour mills and a warehouse, the upper floor was used for living quarters, and a British guard post was built on the roof. Next to the mill there is a lake ('the Mill Lake'), which was created by the nearby dam and from which water was channeled to each grinding station in the Dok mill.

The Current Situation:
Today, the Crusader flour mill Dok is located within the Ein Afek reserve and is a major tourist attraction in the country. The mill itself serves as a museum and visitor center. The main space of the building has been converted into an assembly hall, where a permanent exhibition of traditional agricultural tools is held, and a film is screened every hour on the hour presenting a 'journey' through the reserve. In addition, changing art exhibitions are occasionally displayed in the mill. The reserve has an education and information center for kindergarten children, school students, students in higher education institutions, and more.

Information Status of the Site:
The site has been researched and recorded in archaeological surveys conducted over the years. In 2015, a comprehensive engineering conservation survey was conducted for the three buildings of the mill by conservation engineer Yaakov Sheffer. In addition, there is a conservation plan prepared by Yonatan Orlin in 2023 for the Crusader Dok mill building, along with a detailed documentation file prepared by Sally Gand Maor and Simona Malka.

Description of the Asset and its Surroundings:
The Dok mill was built in the Crusader period in the 12th century, and it includes typical structural elements such as massive stone walls and barrel vaults, built of local kurkar stone and mortar. The mill was built as a fortified structure in the shape of a square. The mill consists of three adjacent buildings, which were built gradually over the years. The mill is built of large stones with diagonal chisel marks typical of the Crusaders. Initially, the mill had three grinding stations, and was later expanded to five grinding units. The ground floor contained flour mills and a warehouse, the upper floor was used for living quarters, and a British guard post was built on the roof. The water from the lake ('the Mill Lake'), created by the adjacent dam, was channeled to the paddle wheels that operated the millstones. The mill is of the chute type, which was typical along streams with a constant flow in the coastal plain. The mill was held by the Templar order until they left the country in the 13th century. During the Ottoman period, the area experienced a renewed flourishing due to the takeover by the Bedouin leader Dhaher al-Omar, who developed Acre and its surroundings and expanded the Dok mill with two new flour grinding stations. During this period, Acre served as the main port of the Land of Israel. During the British Mandate, the flour mill operated until 1925 and served the residents of the area. In 1930, the lake was used as a carp breeding farm by Barkano Ziser. Ziser and a partner leased an area of 90 dunams on the edge of the Kurdani swamp, and dug ponds for fish farming. This attempt was unsuccessful due to a weak water flow, eels that preyed on the fish, and theft by local Arabs. In 1936, the British built the watchtower on the roof of the Dok mill, as part of the events of the Great Arab Revolt. In the years 1937-1947, the place served as one of the first carp farms in the Land of Israel. Today, the state of preservation of the mill is good. The central building has remained relatively intact, and it serves as a testimony to the rich history of the area and the human activity that took place there.
In addition, the Ein Afek reserve contains other important historical components:
Na'aman Stream – The Afek springs are the water source of the Ein Afek Nature Reserve. They are drained through a network of canals to the Na'aman stream, which continues to flow for another 9 km to the north and empties into the Mediterranean Sea.
The Dam – The dam is about 625 m long and 2.5 m high. The dam raised the water level by 7.2 m and created a lake behind it.
The Large Lake and Eshel Pond – The lake is a large body of water that is part of the reserve's landscape. Tamarisk trees and bank vegetation surround the lake. This lake and pond are the remnants of the swamps that were drained in the 20th century.
Tel Afek – An archaeological mound in the southern part of the reserve. Archaeological excavations have revealed remains of human settlement from the Canaanite, Hellenistic, and Roman periods.

The mapping data includes a polygon describing the flour mill building and a line describing the route of the dam wall as it exists on the site today. In addition, a historical road that passed near the mill is marked with a line.

This historical road was the road from Acre to Nazareth. This road leaves Acre and passes near the Na'aman stream and the Dok mill, from there the road continues southeast to Shfaram, passes through the Zippori National Park (formerly the village of Saffuriyya) and descends south to Nazareth. The location and marking of this road were carried out using the P.E.F. map – 1880. The location and marking of the road connecting the Acre-Nazareth road to the mill were carried out using the 1935 map.

properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description: The mill building has undergone conservation and reinforcement in recent years, but it is in a humid environment surrounded by abundant vegetation that could endanger it. Therefore, there is a constant risk of moisture due to capillary rise of water that could damage the rock of the building. In addition, there is a danger of root penetration from plants and trees adjacent to the building as a result of numerous cracks in it. During the conservation process, a constructive reinforcement of the building was carried out by injecting a stabilizing material deep into the walls and filling large cracks. The roof of the building underwent a cladding process that prevents water penetration into the interior spaces of the building. Pruning and cultivation of the vegetation adjacent to the building were carried out to reduce the risk of root penetration into the walls of the building. Finally, the building was reused for a visitor center and therefore cleaning and re-paving were carried out inside the building.

In structure B, which was completed and restored to the highest level, most of the interior walls were plastered. According to the opinion of the architect of the Baháʼí World Centre, there was no conclusive evidence of the existence of plaster on the interior of the building, and therefore it can be said that the decision to plaster the interior walls nevertheless harms the authenticity of the building to some extent. In addition, the wooden access path that leads the visitor between the buildings outlines a single tour route between the buildings and does not reveal all of their parts. This decision was made out of concern for the safety of visitors, as the strength of the floor of some of the buildings is questionable. However, due to the structured tour route of the path, the visitor is not exposed to some of the main parts of the complex, and therefore it can be said that there is damage to his full understanding of the historical function of the complex. Furthermore, the fact that the complex is closed to free public access harms its historical connection with the residents of the city of Acre, who are denied the opportunity to connect with the local heritage of their city. In addition, it should be noted that at the time of the visit to the site by the authors of this text, there was no water in the canals, but it was reported that it was due to return.

The planning boundaries marked on this page were determined because they enclose the entire area between the canals and the mill buildings. We believe that this area is one significant complex and its connection to the other complexes owned by the Baháʼís in the area is of lesser value. This assumption is based on the historical fact that this place functioned as a single unit.
properties.management_data_notes:
The site is owned by the Baháʼí World Centre, however the Israel Antiquities Authority has been accompanying the process of renewal and current functioning of the site for several years. The Ridwan Gardens are not currently open to the general public and are fenced. A dedicated team of gardeners from the Baháʼí World Centre ensures the site's cleanliness and frequent maintenance, as does the garden's guard and his wife who reside permanently on the premises.

In addition, the Acre master plan (G/21535) determined that the site is a conservation complex and therefore the following instructions apply to it:

- The plan will include reference to the immediate surroundings while making an effort to preserve the characteristics of the environment, scale, and character of the construction.

- Sites proposed for conservation in this plan will not be designated for demolition, and trees in the area designated as a conservation site will not be designated for uprooting.

- The plan will include a preliminary documentation file as an accompanying appendix according to the guidelines of the Planning Administration for March 2008.
properties.cultural_assessment_0:
Values:

  • State of preservation - The flour mill complex is unique in its size and state of preservation in the country. 15 pairs of millstones in 5 buildings that operated simultaneously. The relative completeness of the southern facade with a cumulative length of over 75 m expresses the size of the complex and its importance. The site has a variety of different states of preservation that allow the visitor to complete in his imagination what is missing in one building by means of another.
  • Landscape architecture - The mills are an important part of the garden's landscape system, which has landscape and aesthetic qualities. They are placed as a climax at the end of the expansion of the water channels surrounding the garden and are very close to the building where Baháʼu'lláh stayed during his visits to the garden. Together with the Antilia well, the mills create the central axis along which the garden stretches.
  • History - The mills are tangible evidence of the industrial role of the historic Acre-surrounding area. The mills also tell the story of the draining of the Kishon and Na'aman swamps during the 1930s and 40s. Together with the canals and pools that surround them, the mills provide a picture of the landscape that modernism sought to destroy in the first half of the 20th century.
  • Technology - The mills are evidence of a unique technology in the country of flat chute mills that generate their water pressure using only a water head and a slight slope.
  • Spirit and religion – The mills are an integral part of the atmosphere in the garden which provided Baháʼu'lláh with the experience of rest and relaxation, as well as the inspiration for some of the sacred writings of the Baháʼí faith.

Criteria for examining the values:

  • Period - The first documentation of the existence of mills in the area is from the 13th century, while the existing mill buildings in the area can be dated with certainty to the mid-19th century and they definitely constitute a typical building typology for this period.
  • Rarity - The size of the factory, with its number of mills, is exceptional in relation to the other flour mills in the Land of Israel. The method of creating water pressure without a slope of the channel is exceptional in relation to the other chute mills in the Land of Israel.
  • Documentation and findings - The mill buildings themselves are not described in historical sources other than in the description of S. Avitzur. However, several archaeological findings of important historical value were found at the site.
  • Connection to the complex - Being the historical complex of the Ridwan Gardens, a prominent physical monument and the endpoint of its central axis, the mills have an inseparable connection to the gardens' complex.
  • State of preservation - The flour mill complex is unique in its size and state of preservation in the country.
  • Selectivity and diversity – The mills expand the existing diversity in the theme because the use of a channel with such a minimal water head (15 cm!) is unique. Also, the mill complex is the largest known to date in the Land of Israel from the Ottoman period.
  • Potential for future research - As far as we know, the initial construction circumstances of the buildings have not yet been discovered – who built, when, and which parts exactly.

Examination of Authenticity and Completeness:

  • Location - The location of the mills in relation to the garden and in relation to the canals has remained in its original context.
  • Design - The conservation process included the reconstruction of windows, ceilings, and cladding that were destroyed, and therefore there is some damage to authenticity, however the design is based on an attempt to trace the original design.
  • Environment and landscape - The landscape design of the buildings' surroundings is based on the historical description as found in the Baháʼí writings.
  • Materials and construction technologies - In the conservation process, original or close to original materials were mostly used, so that the sense of time and place was preserved.
  • Craftsmanship/Art - The conservation process included the reconstruction of the grinding mechanism and was accompanied by appropriate historical and technological research.
  • Spirit of the place – The spirit of the place was preserved mainly in its landscape context and less in its industrial context.
  • Use and function - Preservation of the garden's role in Baháʼí worship and less in its industrial role.

Statement of Significance-

The mill complex in the Ridwan Gardens is tangible evidence of the industrial role of the historic Acre-surrounding area, and it is unique in its size in relation to flour mills of its kind - in the 'golden age' of the complex it was the largest flour milling factory in the country. The number of mills spread across the site indicates its importance as a first-rate industrial facility for the region's economy. The fact that a technological-industrial factory of a regional level inspired the creation of a 'paradise' in its backyard can serve as a source of inspiration and learning about the human potential inherent in the combination of industry and spirit, which in the case of the flour mills in the Ridwan Gardens, became intertwined.

properties.spirit_of_place: Just as the water canals surround the Ridwan Gardens and create a buffer between it and the outside world, they also create a similar island on which the mill buildings stand. The surroundings of the mills are perceived as a significant expansion in the fabric of the garden as the canals fill the open space. The canals split, surround the cluster of buildings and enter under their vaults, in a way that gives the buildings the image of a rock in the middle of a lake. The new wooden path established as part of the complex's conservation project leads the visitor between and within the buildings on an orderly and prescribed route. Descending from it and wandering freely among the ruins of the buildings, with their various states of preservation, provides a deeper understanding of the operation of the mill factory, so that the visitor can complete in his imagination the missing parts in one building based on what he saw in another. From the garden, the buildings look like an ancient monument that is the climax of the end of the garden, mainly due to the relationship of the canals to it.
properties.description:
In the southern part of the Ridwan Gardens are the remains of 5 flour mill buildings, which housed 15 pairs of millstones. The artificial water canals that fed the mills are located north of the buildings and they are the ones that create the shape of the adjacent Ridwan Gardens. Several bridges cross over the canals. The state of preservation of the buildings varies, some have been destroyed down to the foundation level and some have remained at their full height except for their roofs. During the golden age of the complex, there was one common access to the entire complex (the mills and gardens alike) via the cypress path that comes from the north. With the diversion of the canals and the draining of the swamps, the orientation of the complex changed and a new access road was paved parallel to the eastern diversion canal, so that the cypress avenue to the north served the Baháʼí garden only.

Historical sources indicate that there were flour mills in Acre as early as the Roman period and again in the early Islamic period, and perhaps also in the Crusader period, but their location is unknown. In the 12th century, windmills are mentioned for the first time near Acre and watermills in the following century. Avitzur relates that in 1234 a dispute arose between the Templar Order, which owned the Acre mills, and the Hospitaller Order, which owned the Kurdani mills at Tel Afek, over the water level in the Na'aman stream. On the map of the French survey expedition of 1799, two buildings with the description 'flour mills' appear between the tributaries of the Na'aman stream. In 1875, a plot of land north of the mills was rented by `Abdu'l-Bahá to establish a garden of rest for Baháʼu'lláh, who apparently visited the site for the first time about two years later. Avitzur describes the changes in ownership of the mills among families of Acre residents and even the Waqf. He relates that the factory mainly served the fellahin of the area, and that sometimes they would wait in line for several days. In the mid-1920s, the Palestine Land Development Company purchased the mills with the aim of shutting them down, diverting the waters of the Na'aman, and draining the surrounding swamps, a process that only began towards the end of the 1930s and continued after the establishment of the state. Avitzur, who visited the site in 1955, notes that the former workers of the mills now reside in the buildings themselves. It is not known when they abandoned the site, but it remained desolate until the Baháʼí World Centre commissioned the Israel Antiquities Authority to conduct a survey of the complex in 2006.

After a process of stabilization, partial restoration, and landscape development, the mill complex is now in a high state of preservation, with one building fully completed, its windows and ceiling restored, and an electrical infrastructure installed. Inside, a restored model of the historical grinding mechanism now stands in its original place. The wide water canals have been renovated according to the historical description and although they remain disconnected from the modern Na'aman route, water is pumped into them, once again surrounding the buildings as in the past. The complex is not open to the public except by prior arrangement with the Baháʼí administration of the site and is surrounded by a wall on all sides.

Most of the information about the site is found in the writings of Shmuel Avitzur and in the survey conducted by the Israel Antiquities Authority. Avitzur's contribution deals mainly with the social and economic history of the complex and the contribution of the Israel Antiquities Authority deals mainly with a physical survey and analysis of the complex. Also, to supplement the survey, three seasons of excavations were conducted by the Israel Antiquities Authority, during which pottery, coins, and cannonballs from the time of Napoleon's siege were discovered in the buildings. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that the mills did not operate before the mid-19th century.

The history of the complex can be divided into three main periods. The first period begins with the quarrying of three artificial water canals from the Na'aman stream and the construction of the first three buildings: building A with two mills, building C with two mills, and building E with three mills (according to the division of the Israel Antiquities Authority survey). Later, building C was expanded and another mill was built for it. In the next stage, building D was erected with two mills built with pointed vaults. Later, building E was expanded and one mill was added to it, which was fed by the branching of the canal of building D. Lastly, building B was erected with four mills. The peak size of the complex, when all 15 mills worked simultaneously, coincides with the Baháʼí settlement in the area in the 1870s. All the buildings were built of kurkar stone, but the level of construction varies from building to building, as does the type of wall - single-faced or double-faced. While the latest building, building B, is built in an orderly and meticulous manner, it is evident that buildings C and D have undergone renovations over the years that were done without care for the heights of the floors or the architectural uniformity of the jamb details.
The second period in the history of the complex begins with the purchase of the buildings by the Palestine Land Development Company in the 1920s and the gradual draining of their water canals in several stages. With their purchase, buildings A and E were demolished. In the 1940s, building B was probably the last to function and in the 1950s, when all the mills were out of operation, the original workers still lived in them, who, for the purpose of converting them into residences, poured a layer of concrete on the floors of the buildings.

In the absence of sufficient topographical height or water head, instead of the common chute in the coastal plain mills, horizontal canals were used that become narrower at their ends. In fact, instead of the typical use of gravity to generate energy, the water pressure in these mills was created solely by the water head at the mouth of the canal and a slope of 15 cm at the nozzle – a method unique to this complex.
properties.mapping_description: The original route of the historic Na'aman passed south of the complex and was different from the current route. An artificial canal led the water westward to four canals. From there, the water passed to the five mill buildings and from there it flowed back into the Na'aman route. Of the four canals, the two western ones enclosed an 'island', on which the Ridwan Gardens were established. In addition, the route of the road that led to ancient Acre can be seen in the marking (based on the Palestine Exploration Fund map PEF 1880), which connected with the four canals at their branching point from the artificial canal.
properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
The renewal process of the mill complex included exposing the foundations of the demolished buildings A and E, completing and rebuilding parts of the ruined walls in buildings C and D, removing wild vegetation from inside the buildings, rebuilding the bridges that crossed the canals, opening the clogged canals, building a new wooden walkway that winds between the buildings, restoring and stabilizing some of the arches inside the buildings, restoring the windows and ceiling of building B based on historical research of the remains at the site, and excavating all the original pools and canals around the buildings down to their foundation level, including the application of protective layers and pebbles at the base of the canals to allow for the re-flow of water in them, without, among other things, damaging the base of the buildings.

During the visit of the authors of this document to the site, there was no water in the canals due to maintenance work being done at their base. The site is under frequent monitoring by professionals and maintenance personnel and is closed to the public. For these reasons, it is not subject to any risk other than a visit by a group of Baháʼí believers who are expected to arrive at the site – the site management is preparing to make the site accessible to this audience without causing damage to the buildings.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
The Great Mills complex is a conservation building with values in various fields: architectural, historical, aesthetic, technological, and functional.

Workshops and tours are held at the site from time to time, and it is open to the non-business public.

Although a documentation file that would lead to a conservation file has not yet been created, the mill's managers have an affinity for the worlds of design, aesthetics, and history. In light of this, several 'independent' interventions have been made at the site.

We recommend creating a documentation file that will lead to a conservation file as soon as possible, out of a belief that it would be right to preserve the site's values professionally and, at the same time, to develop an enrichment program aimed at the public in a regulated manner that could include building an educational program with tours, workshops, and lectures for the general public, schools, and students on the history of the mill and its many contexts: architecture, technology, urbanism, the Eretz Israel enterprise, sustainability, and food security, among others.

In light of the visit to the mills and the meeting with the CEO and staff, we believe that the conservation process can take place in cooperation and with the participation of the local people in the practical aspect and as part of identifying additional values that exist at the site.

In this context, we recommend locating other factors connected to the city, including residents of the nearby Wadi Salib neighborhood, and creating a community value identification workshop where operational ideas that can be integrated into the conservation will also be raised.

Another important issue is related to the accessibility of the space: currently, the entrances to the complex are not safe; entry is via the bridge or the road and passes through the parking lot or via stairs. We recommend making the entrance to the complex accessible.

The mill's status is in an industrial area, yet it borders the outskirts of the Wadi Salib neighborhood. We believe that in cooperation with the planning administration, a connection should be created between the complex and the neighborhood – a connection that is also accessible to pedestrians and creates connectivity between the developing lower city and the mill. In this way, the mill can be integrated into the urban fabric, as despite the area's industrial status, it is part of the city.

properties.cultural_assessment_0:
Values:

Historical Value - The Great Mills are among the first modern mills in Israel. At the time of their construction, the mills were considered one of the largest and tallest buildings in the country. The mills represent the beginning of Jewish industry in the Land of Israel and in Haifa and received the support of Baron Edmond de Rothschild. The mills represent a combination and cooperation between two significant figures in the Zionist activity: Edmond de Rothschild and the engineer Arpad Gut, who brought the first concrete mixer to the country. The uniqueness of the mill lies in its urban industrial support based on local Eretz Israel agriculture, aimed at the Jewish settlement in the country and world Jewry.

Aesthetic-Architectural Value - The main building of the mills is an eclectic structure: the body of the building is modernist, made of concrete, with rectangular glass windows and arched windows in the top row. The roof of the building is decorated with local turret-like elements in a local style. In addition, the engineer Gut insisted that in every wall, the floor and ceiling would support themselves without supporting columns, thus allowing for flexibility in the placement of machinery and equipment in the work halls.

Alongside the industrial building, the 'Miller's House' is in a local European style with a tiled roof and a back orchard.

As mentioned, the mills were planned and designed by the engineer Arpad Gut, who was responsible for many public and industrial buildings in the early settlement period; this was his first major project in the country.

Urban Landscape Value - At the time of its construction, the mill building had a significant presence in the urban landscape from the sea and railway line and from the landscape line of Wadi Salib.

The mills are located on a major road axis near the historic railway line and today's Highway 4, and are close to the port and other industrial buildings.

The mills are in the range between city and sea, between the residential city and the industrial area and the port.

In the mill complex, behind the 'Miller's House', there is an orchard that they wish to restore.

Connection to Fabric or Complex – The Great Mills are part of the urban fabric of the lower city, which until the mid-1930s was the center of urban life in Haifa. The railway was established in the area where other industrial factories developed, and later the new Haifa ports (British and Chinese) were established there. The mills are on significant transportation axes: railway, port, Highway 4, and for pedestrians, a bridge was built crossing the main road.

Use Value - The Great Mills continue to operate as one of the largest flour mills in the country. Alongside flour milling and packaging, baking workshops, tours by request, and art events are held at the site, inviting the local creative community and the general public to get to know the place and its activities.

Scientific/Technological Value - Use of new industrial technology. A modern flour mill based on a gasoline engine with innovative tools.

Research Potential - The Great Mills are a significant and interesting focus in urban and national development, with historical, contemporary, aesthetic, and cultural values. However, there is no research about them. We believe that there is great value in researching the mill complex itself, in its urban, national, and regional context in light of changing times. We believe that this research can provide tools for future spatial development.

Examination of Authenticity and Completeness / State of Preservation:

The Great Mills are active flour mills to this day. The main building is largely preserved in its materiality and design, the windows are original, and the mill's inscription, which was visible from a distance, still exists but is worn and faded. Alongside this, elevators have been added, and the original machinery has been replaced over the years in the name of progress. The original silos of the mill, to which the mill was required to add additions in the form of grids by the insurance company. In the 1950s, the main silo was added, followed by six more round silos over the years. The Miller's House, which is now the office building, was divided and adapted, as were the workshop rooms, but it seems that these are not irreversible changes. However, at this stage, the ability to validate has not been proven with high probability.

Statement of Significance:

The Great Mills in Haifa were established in 1922 and are among the first modern, industrial, diesel-engine based flour mills in the country. The mills, founded by the JCA[1] with the support of Baron Rothschild and designed by the engineer Arpad Gut, are an interesting case study of their work in building the country.

The building is known for its special architectural qualities as an industrial concrete structure in an eclectic style that combines a modern rectangular structural base with local oriental finishes, windows, decorations, and openings. In this context, the building illuminates the work of the engineer Gut, who is identified with many public and industrial buildings during the Mandate period, and the connection between aesthetics and technology in modern local architecture.

The mills represent the beginning of material and technological innovation in the country. They are among the first buildings in the country built of reinforced concrete and among the first mills based on a diesel engine, and are a symbol of Haifa and Eretz Israel modernism.

The mills were built on the outskirts of the Wadi Salib neighborhood on a main road axis near the Palestine Railway and close to the port. They had high landscape visibility and were identified with the Haifa landscape, and in the 1920s the mill was considered one of the largest buildings in the country. The Great Mills are identified with the beginning of Haifa and Eretz Israel industry.

The location of the mills on an urban-national and regional road axis represents an important stage in Haifa's history, in which Haifa took a significant part in the network of cities of Bilad al-Sham and was a significant axis in the connection between Palestine/Land of Israel and the West.

The Great Mills complex is an important and interesting case study in Jewish settlement before the establishment of the state. It combines an economic, industrial, agricultural enterprise with urban, national, and regional significance. The mills provided work for the country's farmers and workers in Haifa and the region, while the flour milled there was sold in local markets in the country and to world Jewry.

The history of the Great Mills is intertwined with the history of Jewish settlement in the country and in the State of Israel through the establishment of an industrial-agricultural-urban enterprise, the Jewish-Palestinian national conflict, the privatization of factories, and the turn to a global market alongside local activity.

Today, the 'Great Mills' mill continues to operate as a flour mill within the 'Great Mills of Eretz Israel' group. Workshops, tours, and art events are held at the site.

The mills are located on a central axis but do not realize their potential as a connecting complex in the urban fabric. We believe that architectural, historical, technological, and cultural conservation as part of a regional plan will contribute greatly to urban development.

[1] In Yiddish: 'Yiddishe Kolonizatzia Asosiatzie', from English: J.C.A; acronym for Jewish Colonization Association; in Hebrew translation: 'The Jewish Colonization Association', in 1924 JCA would become PICA - Palestine Jewish Colonization Association.

properties.description:
The History of the Mill

The 'Great Mills' in Haifa was the first modern flour mill established in the Land of Israel. The mill, located in Haifa, was established at the beginning of the British Mandate in 1921 at the initiative of Baron Rothschild, with construction beginning in 1921 and completed by September 1922. The building was then among the largest buildings in the Land of Israel for its time. In July 1923, the mill's wheels were driven by then-innovative diesel engines. The mill is considered the first modern mill in the country to be operated by diesel, importing the most advanced machinery from Switzerland.

The steam engine was part of the industrial revolution, and the great flour mills represent another point in the beginning of the Eretz Israel and Haifa industry in general.

The mill was established at the initiative of Baron Edmond James de Rothschild, as part of his support for the Zionist enterprise and settlement. Rothschild hoped to create an infrastructure for Eretz Israel industry and, at the same time, to help the farmers in the Land of Israel to establish themselves on agricultural work and to enable them to sell their produce for a fair wage, and in addition to help sell the agricultural produce from Israel abroad.

The mill was located in a strategic location near the railway line on a main road in the developing Wadi Salib neighborhood, with the railway line leading into the mill's courtyard to facilitate loading and unloading. In old photographs, the mill building is seen to occupy a dominant place in the urban skyline.

The Hungarian-Jewish architect and engineer Arpad Gut, who specialized in reinforced concrete and is responsible for significant architectural projects, was chosen for the mill construction project. Gut specialized in reinforced concrete construction and bridge building; he brought the first concrete mixer to the country with him. In Hungary, he planned and managed projects of industrial buildings and factories. In the country, he continued his work and is responsible, among other things, for the Gali Aviv Casino in Tel Aviv, the Great Synagogue on Allenby, the water tower on Mazeh Street, and other factories in Haifa, including the Kishon workshops - the railway workshops in the Haifa Bay.

In an article that refers specifically to the flour mills in Ashdod, the architect Michael Jacobson writes that the industrial revolution, which reached its peak at the beginning of the 20th century, tightened the ties between industry and architecture and especially between technology and design. In those years, the Eretz Israel industry was admittedly in its infancy, but like their European counterparts, the local industrialists paid great attention to architecture.

Over the years, the mill underwent changes, most of them related to expansions and the replacement of machinery with newer and more advanced models. The mill continues to operate to this day, grinding wheat grains that arrive from the Dagon silos, and is considered among the largest and highest quality flour mills in the country.

The Technology of Modern Flour Mills:

The main processing machines of a flour milling plant like the Great Mills in Haifa include flour milling equipment, screening equipment, and a flour purifier.

Flour Processing Stages in Modern Mills:

First stage: Transporting the grains from the port to the mill complex, previously done by rail, today done by trucks that enter and exit the mill complex to Highway 4. The grain from abroad arrives at the mill when the truck's contents are unloaded into a 'receiver' and then transferred to storage in silos until milling is required.

Second stage: In the initial stages of treatment, the grains undergo a cleaning process from large impurities in a machine that separates the different grains as shown in the diagram below: (A) The grain falls onto an adjustable plate (B), which directs it onto a rotating coil (C). Impurities too large to pass through the wire mesh are transferred and fall onto a smaller coil (D), which extracts any grain carried by the impurities. Grain from the coil (C) falls onto the sealing gate (E) and out of the machine at (F). Air is drawn through the stream of grain and carries light impurities through (G) to the settling chamber (H). The air passes to the fan inlet (J) and is discharged from the fan back into the machine.

Third stage: After cleaning and separation, the grain is broken down on 'break rolls' and sifted in special machines, after which the flour passes to reduction rolls with smooth or finely grooved surfaces. The rolls are made of chilled cast iron. The number of grooves, or flutes, in a roll varies from about ten per centimeter in the first 'break' rolls to about twenty-five in the rolls used in the fourth and final break operation. The flutes are not cut parallel to the axis, but in a slight spiral.

Fourth stage: Screening machines - After the grain has passed through the break rolls, the screens extract the coarser stock before it is purified. Such as bran, flour, and semolina. The screens grade and separate these products for other treatment. The sieves of a sifter of this type, as demonstrated here, are arranged in nests and can be easily pulled out for inspection while the machine is running. The sieves perform a rotary motion in a horizontal plane. The machine is supported by groups of flexible canes suspended from the ceiling. The flour is fed through fabric sleeves at the top of the machine, and the sifted products are separated and discharged from sleeves at the bottom of the machine.

Timeline

1921-1922 Establishment of the mill at the initiative of Rothschild, owned by PICA (JCA), planned by engineer Arpad Gut.

1923 - The mill operates and grinds flour using diesel-based engine technology.

1923/1924 - Koshering of the mill for Passover (in the 1923 press): aroused resentment among the small mills that focused on grinding flour for Passover, and as a result, the Chief Rabbinate refrained from intervening in the matter of the mill's certification and the ways of certifying such a large mill, leaving the matter in the hands of the rabbi of Haifa, Rabbi Baruch Marcus.

1925 - Establishment of the Beit Hahoreshet/matzah factory adjacent to the mill. The factory was built by Solel Boneh.

April 1948 - Repeated attacks to blow up the mill.

1952 - The PICA management decided to renovate, expand, and improve the factory, and to add a large grain silo, the construction of which began that same year. In an article from that year, it is noted that the mills were among the largest factories in the country and in the Middle East that gave a boost to the economic development of Haifa.

1954 - Sale of the mills to private ownership.

Today: The mill is owned by the Hefetz family, the mill continues to operate as a flour mill where baking workshops are held and art events are occasionally held.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
Conservation recommendations and policy for the Sakhne flour mill focus on an accurate restoration of the structure and technological systems, alongside routine maintenance of the site and preservation of its natural environment. It is recommended to incorporate an experiential guided tour for visitors and ensure full accessibility for all types of populations, all while maintaining sustainability and preserving the historical and natural heritage of the place.

The considerations for determining the boundaries and planning recommendations for the conservation of the flour mill site at Gan HaShlosha include a wide range of environmental, historical, technological, and community factors:

  • Historical and Cultural Considerations:

One of the main considerations was the authentic preservation of the building and the technology used in it. Since the mill is part of the historical heritage of the area, it was necessary to preserve the stone structure, the hydraulic milling technology, and the natural system of water and the dam.

The contribution of the mill to community life throughout the periods should also be considered, with an emphasis on the period of Zionist settlement and 'Tower and Stockade', when this area served as a source of inspiration and agricultural determination.

  • Environmental Considerations:

The site's location within Gan HaShlosha Park and the Nahal Amal Reserve requires maintaining the ecological balance of the place. The boundaries were chosen to preserve the natural ecological systems such as the flow of water from the Sakhne springs, the preservation of local flora and fauna, and the prevention of damage to nature as a result of human use.

It must be ensured that the buildings and conservation do not harm the natural flow of water from the stream or the nearby springs.

  • Technological Considerations:

As part of the conservation, it was necessary to preserve various mechanical parts of the mill, such as the paddle wheels, water channels, and ancient technological systems, while protecting the structure from erosion and natural wear.

Modern technologies were used to reinforce the structure, especially for protection against earthquakes, with the planning boundaries chosen so that the place could maintain its stability over time.

  • Access and Sustainable Conservation Considerations:

Public access considerations were an important component in determining the planning boundaries, especially regarding making the site accessible to people with disabilities. This required creating accessible paths and additional buildings that would be suitable for mass visits, all without harming the historical and environmental value of the site.

In addition, sustainability considerations, such as the use of solar energy and water recycling, were a central consideration in the planning, with the aim of making the site sustainable while preventing the waste of resources.

  • Community and Educational Considerations:

The place is intended to serve not only as a tourist attraction but also as an educational center. This consideration included planning areas for guidance and educational activities around historical, cultural, and ecological topics, which influenced the setting of the boundaries of the area designated for conservation.

These considerations express the desire to combine the preservation of the mill's history and technology, the preservation of the natural ecological system, and making the place accessible to the general public while emphasizing long-term sustainability.

Focused Conservation Recommendations for the Sakhne Flour Mill Site:

Accurate Architectural and Operational Restoration:

Stone Structure: The original stone structure of the mill should be preserved, while preserving the authentic building materials, such as local stone and natural plaster.

Water System: The water system that powered the flour mill is largely preserved and restored. The water from the springs that was the driving force of the mill remains essential to the site's experience. It is recommended to maintain the system by regularly checking the water channels, the mill wheels, and the dam structure.

Routine Maintenance:

Continuous maintenance of the mill parts must be carried out, with an emphasis on the wear of the mechanical parts (such as the gears) due to the flow of water. The maintenance will include protecting the structure from natural wear, such as the erosion of stones or the accumulation of invasive vegetation around the channels.

It must be ensured that the rest of the site is preserved and clean, and also to ensure that visitors preserve the area and prevent damage to the local vegetation or the historical structure.

Historical and Technological Preservation:

It is important to preserve the structure in a way that preserves the original use of the mill and presents it to the general public in an interactive way. The mill should be operated during guided tours, or through technological simulations, to demonstrate how the mechanism worked in practice.

Preservation of the Ecological System:

The site is located within a nature reserve of Nahal Amal, which must be preserved both in terms of cleanliness and in terms of preserving biodiversity. The flow of the stream should not be altered or the nearby springs damaged in order to preserve the natural conditions that allow the mill to operate.

Recommendations for Operation and Accessibility:

Visitor Guidance:

It is recommended to provide organized guidance or guided tours that explain the history of the place, the process of the mill's operation, and its economic and social significance during the period in which it operated.

Clear informative signage and explanation stations along the route should be provided to help visitors understand the importance of the mill and the history of the area.

Accessibility for People with Disabilities:

It must be ensured that the site is also accessible to people with disabilities, including easy access to all parts of the site, accessible bridges over the water channels, and interactive signage adapted for an audience with special needs.

Sustainable Conservation:

A policy of sustainable conservation should be encouraged by operating the mill and park areas in a way that prevents the waste of resources and preserves the natural environment. For example, by using alternative energy systems that can assist in the site's maintenance. Here are some concrete recommendations for accessibility and sustainable conservation of the flour mill at Gan HaShlosha, focusing on preventing the waste of resources and preserving the natural environment:

  1. Installation of Solar Systems: Advanced solar systems can be installed on the roofs of buildings or in adjacent areas to generate clean energy for the site's operation, such as outdoor lighting, water pumps, and ventilation systems. This will reduce the use of electricity from polluting sources and create a renewable and environmentally friendly energy source.
  2. Water Recycling: In order to reduce water consumption, it is recommended to integrate a system for recycling the stream water used to operate the mill. The system will be able to route the water after use back into the cycle, while filtering and cleaning the water as needed, thus preventing the waste of precious water.
  3. Natural Materials and Sustainable Construction: To preserve the ancient and natural buildings, natural materials and ecological construction methods should be used. The use of lime plaster and local stones can contribute both to the preservation of the original structure and to the prevention of environmental damage from the use of synthetic materials.
  4. Installation of Accessible and Resource-Efficient Paths: Planning accessible access paths using natural materials such as wood or stone will reduce the impact on the environment and increase accessibility for people with disabilities. The use of recycled materials or materials with a green standard will contribute to sustainable conservation.
  5. Guidance on Environmental Preservation: Educational activities and guidance for visitors on the importance of environmental and historical preservation should be integrated. The wise use of water, energy, and resources in nature can be emphasized as part of the preservation of the mill and the park.
  6. Drainage and Rainwater Management Systems: Improving the drainage systems and infiltrating rainwater into the ground will help preserve natural water reservoirs while reducing the risk of structural damage caused by the accumulation of water around the buildings.
  7. Visitor Load Control: To prevent damage from the accumulation of too large a crowd in sensitive areas, visitor load control systems such as queues and stopping stations in different areas should be implemented, and the number of visitors allowed to enter certain parts of the site at the same time should be limited.

This policy will not only help in the long-term preservation of the mill, but will also contribute to the visitor experience and the preservation of the natural environment around Gan HaShlosha.

Based on what we mentioned above, there are several aspects in the conservation recommendations for the flour mill at Gan HaShlosha that are not currently fully implemented, and it is important to add them to the routine activities:

  1. Installation of Solar Systems: It does not appear that solar systems have already been installed for the operation of the site. This is an important recommendation, as solar systems can provide clean energy and reduce the use of electricity from polluting sources. This addition will contribute to making the site sustainable and will improve its maintenance.
  2. Water Recycling System: The recommendation to integrate a system for recycling the stream water has not yet been implemented. The installation of such a system could reduce the waste of water, which is an important resource in the place, and would allow for its reuse for various needs such as demonstrations or maintenance of the systems.
  3. Full Accessibility for People with Disabilities: The issue of making the site accessible to people with disabilities still requires further development. It is recommended to add accessible paths and adapt bridges over the water channels, along with interactive signage for an audience with special needs, in order to ensure an accessible visiting experience for all populations.
  4. Educational Activities and Environmental Guidance: Although the place is used for certain educational activities, there is a need to expand the guidance on environmental preservation, sustainable conservation, and local history, while emphasizing the wise use of water and energy as an important resource.
  5. Improvement of Drainage and Rainwater Management System: According to the recommendations, improving the drainage systems and rainwater infiltration could prevent future damage to the building as a result of water accumulation. This is an area that does not seem to exist at the moment and should be considered for addition to protect the mill.

In general, the recommended policy is to combine historical preservation with environmental preservation and advanced technologies, while ensuring full accessibility and educational experiences for the general public.
properties.management_data_notes:
Site Management

  1. Israel Nature and Parks Authority: The Israel Nature and Parks Authority is responsible for managing the site, including maintenance, conservation, and operation for the public. It is the body that carries out conservation and maintenance activities for historical structures like the flour mill, manages conservation budgets, and directs pedagogical and educational activities at the site.
  2. Conservation of Historical Buildings: Conservation work at the site is carried out under the supervision of the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, in collaboration with the Council for Conservation of Heritage Sites in Israel, the Israel Antiquities Authority, and the Museum of Regional Mediterranean Archaeology, bodies that work to preserve and restore historical sites throughout the country. The council specializes in architectural and mechanical conservation work, ensuring the preservation of the original character of the buildings.
  3. Conservation and Development Work:
    • Conservation Contractors and Professionals: Conservation is carried out by contractors and professionals who specialize in the restoration and conservation of historical buildings. These are architects and engineers who specialize in working with ancient stone structures and restoring water infrastructure.
    • Restoration of Mechanical Systems: Experts in historical mechanics work on restoring the systems that powered the mill. Some of the water and grinding systems have been rebuilt based on historical knowledge and research.
  4. Site Operation and Education: The site staff includes guides and operators who specialize in guiding groups and visitors, and who conduct educational activities and historical tours of the place. There are also special events and workshops that explain the historical importance of the site and the conservation process.
  5. Cooperation with Local Bodies:
    The site cooperates with local bodies such as the Valley of Springs Regional Council, which functions as part of the conservation and tourism development of the area. The council participates in various aspects of site conservation and upgrading and tourist activities.

Funding for Conservation and Development

  • Funding for the conservation of the flour mill comes from several sources:
    • Government budget that comes through the Israel Nature and Parks Authority and the Council for Conservation of Heritage Sites.
    • Revenues from visitor entrance fees to the site are also used for the development and maintenance of the site.
    • Sometimes there are collaborations with private entities or donations intended for the purposes of conservation and development of the site.

Challenges in Management and Conservation

The site, being a combination of history and nature, requires a delicate balance between preserving heritage and protecting the surrounding ecological system. The Israel Nature and Parks Authority faces these challenges, such as:

  • Natural wear and tear of buildings and stones due to weather conditions and water flow.
  • Managing the flow of visitors while preserving the physical and natural environment.
  • Ecological conservation: Preserving the natural water sources of Nahal Amal and coordinating with environmental bodies to maintain the quality of the water and nature.

In general, the site is under continuous management and supervision of certified conservation bodies, whose purpose is to ensure that the buildings and the natural environment are preserved for future generations.
properties.cultural_assessment_0:
Cultural Assessment of the Site and Mill at Gan HaShlosha

The cultural assessment of Gan HaShlosha and its historic mill stems from the combination of historical importance, national symbolism, and natural beauty. The place represents several important layers of Israeli and regional culture:

1. Historical and National Heritage: The flour mill at Gan HaShlosha is directly linked to the Zionist settlement and the principles of the 'Tower and Stockade' enterprise in the 1920s and 1930s. The 'Tower and Stockade' project was born out of the need to quickly establish Jewish settlements in strategic areas, especially in threatened regions like the Beit She'an Valley. The establishment of the settlements was a response to the political and security pressures of the period, and they were built within a few days using temporary structures surrounded by a wall.

Kibbutz Nir David (Tel Amal), near Gan HaShlosha, was the first 'Tower and Stockade' settlement established in 1936, and it symbolizes the beginning of the settlement process in the Beit She'an Valley. Gan HaShlosha and the mill, located nearby, are part of this national story, as they illustrate the strong connection between the land, water, and agriculture to the settlement enterprise. The use of the Sakhne spring water and the hydraulic flour mill connects the technological past of flour milling, representing traditional agriculture, with the Zionist determination to build the land, establish settlements, and defend them. The national heritage of the mill stems from its being a symbol of how the Zionist settlement enterprise was based on deep agricultural roots, while preserving ancient traditions and integrating advanced technologies for their time, such as hydraulic milling. This meeting between the historical past, expressed in the use of water power for milling, and the Zionist present, in which new kibbutzim and moshavim were built, is a foundation in the shaping of Israeli national identity.

2. Historical Importance: The mill is a symbol of the different periods that the region has undergone — from the Ottoman period, through the Mandate period, to the early days of the state. It illustrates the historical connection between water, agriculture, and settlement in the Beit She'an Valley. The site today is a fascinating perspective on the daily lives of the early inhabitants, on the challenges they faced, and on the creative ways they dealt with environmental conditions to create sources of food and local industry.

3. Educational and Touristic Value: Gan HaShlosha, with its historic mill, serves not only as a tourist attraction but also as an educational site for students, tourists, and researchers. The place allows learning about local and national history, alongside experiential experiences in nature. The conservation of the flour mill and its transformation into a tourist attraction emphasize its cultural importance, both historically and as a place of learning. Here are some examples of educational activities that take place at the site:

Guided Tours: Tours are held that combine historical explanations about the settlement periods in the area, especially about the Zionist settlement and the 'Tower and Stockade' enterprise. Visitors learn how agricultural technologies, such as hydraulic flour mills, were used by farmers in that period.

Agricultural and Handicraft Workshops: As part of the educational activities, participants can take part in workshops where they experience ancient agricultural work methods. For example, they learn about the operation of flour milling using a small manual mill reconstruction or about baking bread using traditional methods.

Nature and Environmental Studies: Alongside history, the site encourages learning about the environmental importance of preserving the natural water sources of the area. Students and visitors learn about the role of the mill in the local agricultural history and the connection between water resources and renewable energy technologies.

Experiential Activities in Nature: In addition to theoretical learning, field activities are held that combine walking along the Sakhne water channels, nature tours, and getting to know the unique ecological system of the area, including the hot springs, natural pools, and surrounding vegetation.

National History and Settlement: There is a focus on teaching the history of the Zionist settlement and the construction of 'Tower and Stockade' settlements. The activity combines a visit to the nearby 'Tower and Stockade' museum, and helps to understand the connection between the agricultural heritage of flour mills and the processes of Zionist settlement in the Beit She'an Valley.

These activities encourage an experiential connection between nature, history, and the heritage of the land, and make the visit to Gan HaShlosha a valuable educational experience.

4. Natural Aesthetics: Alongside the historical aspects, Gan HaShlosha is considered one of the most beautiful places in the country. The combination of natural water, permanent springs, and the green landscape gives it a high aesthetic value, which adds to its cultural appreciation as a unique and relaxing leisure area.

5. Community and Human Symbolism: The flour mill is a testament to the culture of hard work and agriculture that was common in the area hundreds of years ago. It recalls not only the agricultural past but also the community and joint work that were required to operate the mill. It is a symbol of a cooperative culture that developed in that area in ancient times and continued into the Zionist period.

In general, Gan HaShlosha and the mill are an important part of Israeli heritage, and reflect the combination of nature, history, and culture that make the place a national asset.
