The spirit of the place at Gan HaShlosha carries with it a deep connection between nature, history, and Israeli culture. The place is located in the environment of Nahal Amal (Asi) which flows through Gan HaShlosha, and is considered one of the most beautiful places in the country due to its natural pools, lush vegetation, and the pastoral landscape of the valley. The water flowing all year round at a pleasant temperature has created a meeting point for nature, agriculture, and history. Gan HaShlosha symbolizes the struggle of the Zionist settlement at the beginning of the 20th century, with the establishment of the first settlements as part of the plan to establish 'Tower and Stockade' settlements, including Tel Amal (today Nir David) which was established in one night in 1936.

The feeling at the place combines an experience of relaxation and natural beauty with a sense of historical rootedness. Visitors can bathe in the springs, walk along the stream, be impressed by the open landscape of the Valley of Springs, and feel the Israeli history and ancient times, which are also reflected through the archaeological museum at the site. The flour mill is living evidence of the agricultural heritage of the area, where water was not only a natural resource but also a source of life and economy. The spirit of the place expresses the historical tradition of flour milling using water energy and illustrates the connection between man and nature through agricultural work. In addition, the ancient structure itself, with its stone walls and grinding wheels, evokes a sense of respect for the historical production methods that served the communities of the area for generations.

Today, the place serves as a cultural and educational attraction, allowing visitors to be exposed to the history of the valley, to understand life in the Ottoman and Mandate periods, and to experience the ancient technologies of agriculture and flour milling. The open-air museum and education programs at the site help in a deeper understanding of the area and its cultural and national importance. The spirit of the place at Gan HaShlosha and the flour mill radiates natural tranquility, historical resilience, and a connection to Zionist ideals. The place combines natural beauty with historical value, and allows visitors to experience the past in a tangible way, while enjoying the landscape and connecting to the land and the cultural roots of the area.
properties.description:
The flour mill at Gan HaShlosha is a historic building located within a national park in the Beit She'an Valley, in the north of the country. The mill was built during the Ottoman period, probably at the end of the 19th or beginning of the 20th century. The building is made of local stone and consists of several rooms, the main one being the room where the flour milling equipment stood. The flour mill was operated by the energy of the water flowing from Nahal Amal (Asi), a natural water source that provides a constant flow throughout the year.

The Sakhne springs provided water for drinking, agriculture, and the operation of technological facilities such as flour mills. Flour mills were once a central part of the economy and daily life of the residents of rural areas, and were the main means of grinding grains to produce flour. The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, as evidenced by various archaeological finds. In biblical and more ancient times, the Beit She'an Valley was an important transit point for trade and transportation, as well as an important agricultural center.

Flour Mill Technology

A combination of a chimney system and a chute system: The mill was operated by a hydraulic system that utilized the flow of water from Nahal Amal. The flowing water passed through chimneys to a large water wheel located in the water, which drove the millstones to grind the grains. This was a common and efficient method at that time. In addition, this specific mill had a combination of a chute mill method. This combination characterized the mill. In addition, the mechanical system included millstones that were driven by water power and ground the grain into flour. The millstones were also used for other purposes such as grinding spices, and were made of hard stone that ensured durability over time.

The construction system of the mill included several important components that were interconnected, and they described a classic architectural structure of a hydraulic mill.

Architectural Features: The structure combines traditional local building styles, with the use of thick stone walls and grinding facilities that worked by water power. Arches and durable stone walls are among the main components of the mill, which are an example of the simple and durable architecture of the Ottoman period.

Construction Methods: The mill was built of local stone and designed to withstand the pressures of the flow and daily work. The walls were particularly thick, and the entire structure was built to remain stable for many years.

Components of the Mill and their Function:

The Dam: A structure whose function was to store water from the stream and direct it into the aqueduct that led the water towards the mill. The dam was a critical part of ensuring a stable flow of water to the mill.

The Bridge: A crossing over the stream that was built as part of the operational system of the mill. The bridge was used to transport materials and equipment from one side of the complex to the other, and possibly also as an access structure to the aqueduct and other components of the mill.

The Pool: A storage basin built near the mill, where the water was stored before being channeled into the mill through the aqueduct. The water in the pool served as a source of energy to drive the paddle wheels.

The Aqueduct: A channel or pipe that led the water from the pool into the grinding system in the mill. Its design was critical, as it had to lead the water precisely to allow a sufficiently strong flow of water to drive the paddle wheels.

The Chimney: A vertical channel through which the water was poured with force into the paddle wheels. The flow of water falling through the chimney drove the wheels that were connected to the grinding system on the grinding floor.

The Chute: A channel in which the water flows back to the stream after passing through the paddle wheels and driving them. The chute was designed to ensure a return flow of water to the natural system.

Paddle Wheel Vaults: Arches that contained the paddle wheels themselves. The wheels were arranged inside the vaults, and the flow of water inside the vault created the necessary movement to drive the grinding system.

Grinding Floor Vaults: The floor where the grinding operation itself was carried out, by means of millstones that moved thanks to the energy produced by the paddle wheels. The grinding floor also included a system for sorting and transferring the flour.

The Connections between the Components

The components in the mill were connected and functioned harmoniously to create an efficient grinding system. The water from the dam was stored in the pool and from there it was channeled through the aqueduct to the chimney, which fell through the paddle wheel vaults, and the wheels drove the millstones on the grinding floor. Each component in this system was essential for producing flour efficiently and without dependence on external energy sources.

The hydraulic design of the system made these flour mills a powerful tool for the local settlements, and yet their preservation in their original condition is a challenge of many years.

Historical Summary: Flour mills were an integral part of daily life in the Ottoman period and were an essential means of grinding grains into flour for making bread and other products. The mill at Gan HaShlosha served the residents of the area for many years, until the beginning of the 20th century, when new technologies began to replace traditional flour mills. The owners of the historic mill were probably from local farming families in the area during the Ottoman period, residents of the village of Faqqu'a on the Gilboa. The mill primarily served the Arab fellahin and the communities in the area and met the needs of local agriculture, mainly by utilizing the water of Nahal Amal for flour milling.

During the Mandate period, new Zionist settlements were established in the area as part of the Zionist settlement enterprise. Over the years, the use of the traditional mill was gradually discontinued, and in the period after the establishment of the state, it became a historical site. In recent decades, efforts have been made to preserve the mill and make it part of the open-air museum at Gan HaShlosha, which is dedicated to the history of settlement in the Land of Israel and the agricultural heritage of the area.

The Ottoman Period

During the Ottoman period, flour mills were a necessary asset for every village and agricultural area, as they provided the most basic product: flour for bread, the main food of the inhabitants of the country. The location of the mill at Gan HaShlosha was optimal in terms of proximity to natural water sources, with an emphasis on Nahal Amal (Asi), which served as the main energy source for the mill. The construction of flour mills along rivers and streams was common, as it allowed for continuous operation, without the need for a large labor force.

The Mandate Period and Zionism

With the beginning of Zionist settlement in the Beit She'an Valley in the 1920s and 1930s, the mill became an important service for the new settlements established as part of the 'Tower and Stockade' settlement project, including the nearby Kibbutz Nir David. The mill was part of a local food production system that helped the new Jewish communities to be agriculturally independent.

The Decline in the Use of Flour Mills during the Mid-20th Century, with the advent of modern technologies and industrial progress, the use of hydraulic flour mills like the one at Gan HaShlosha declined. The traditional mills were replaced by mechanized flour mills and industrial plants, and the mill ceased to operate regularly.

Its Transformation into a Historical Site. The mill at Gan HaShlosha was preserved and became a historical site as part of the efforts to preserve the heritage of the Zionist settlement and the agricultural history of the area. Over the years, conservation and restoration work was carried out on it, and it was opened to the public as part of the open-air museum at Gan HaShlosha, which is dedicated to the study of the history of settlement in the Land of Israel.
properties.mapping_description:
The mill is located within the Gan HaShlosha National Park, in the valley area of the Beit She'an Valley, in the Lower Galilee. Its strategic location on Nahal Amal allowed it to operate for many years without the need for external energy sources. The site is located near the Sakhne springs at the Gan HaShlosha site, which is a popular natural water source, known for its clear and warm water. The Valley of Springs is located between the Gilboa mountains to the west and the Jordan River to the east.

The Establishment of Gan HaShlosha and Planning by Architects

Gan HaShlosha (the Sakhne) was established in the 1930s, with the architectural planning and design carried out by three main architects: Avraham Yahalom, Shlomo Bahir, and Leopold Krakauer. They planned the garden with the aim of combining the unique natural features of the area with a harmonious landscape architectural design, which would allow enjoyment of the water sources and preservation of the natural and historical heritage of the place.

The flour mill is located on Nahal Amal (the Sakhne), and covers a relatively small area. It is a historic stone building, which was used for grinding flour using the power of the water flowing from the stream. The mill at Gan HaShlosha is part of a historical-agricultural system that includes the facilities and the surrounding area, such as the dam, water channels, and pools.

Next to the mill was a dam whose function was to stop and regulate the flow of water from Nahal Amal, and to allow its accumulation in order to utilize its power for grinding flour. The dam directed the water to water channels that were used to transport the water to the mill wheels. These channels were constructed channels that were built in order to efficiently utilize the amount of water that flowed in the stream.

Channels and Pools: The channels led the water to small storage pools, and from here the water was poured with a sufficiently strong flow to drive the grinding wheels that were installed inside the building. The pools were also used for other purposes such as irrigation and meeting other agricultural needs, which were very important in the agricultural economy of the period.

Importance of the System: This system not only served the mill, but was part of a larger water system that served the residents of the area, including agricultural and industrial needs. Nahal Amal was a central water source for many uses, including for other flour mills in the area.

The Location of the Sakhne in Israeli Culture

The Sakhne, with its hot springs and the green landscape surrounding it, has over the years become a cultural site of great importance in the Israeli consciousness. The place is a symbol of family trips, recreation in nature, and a meeting point between different communities. It is identified with childhood experiences and is considered one of the scenic gems of Israel. The place has also been mentioned in songs and literature, which emphasizes its place in popular culture.

The Sakhne is also considered a site of Jewish and agricultural heritage, with a direct connection to the Zionist settlement enterprise in the Beit She'an Valley and the activities of the kibbutzim and moshavim in the area. The place represents the combination of a thriving natural landscape and the cultural and social heritage of Zionist settlement in the Land of Israel.

Uniqueness of the Natural and Historical Data

The Hot Springs: The Sakhne is characterized by natural springs with a constant temperature of about 28 degrees Celsius all year round, which makes it one of the special places in the country that allows bathing even in the winter season. This water originates from deep layers of soil and has high concentrations of minerals that feed the stream and the pools.

Abundance of Water: The clear water that comes from the hot springs feeds the natural pools and waterfalls at the site, and they are a major attraction for tourists and hikers. The combination of clear water and the green surroundings creates an extraordinary experience of a thriving natural landscape in the heart of a relatively hot and dry area like the Beit She'an Valley.

Ancient History: The site, in addition to its unique natural resources, includes the aforementioned flour mill, historical agricultural facilities from various periods, remains of ancient settlement, and also finds from the Roman and Byzantine periods. The historical system of flour mills and water channels symbolizes the use of water power throughout the generations, which strengthens the historical value of the place.

Interesting and Special at the Sakhne

Beyond the uniqueness of the water and nature, the Sakhne combines a rich and diverse landscape with a rich history. The connection between the natural abundance and the agricultural and historical heritage of the area makes Gan HaShlosha one of the most fascinating sites in the country. The fact that the garden has preserved its naturalness over the years, with minimal development and preservation of the open landscape, allows for an authentic nature experience for visitors. The Sakhne not only offers a green landscape and hot water, but also a deep historical and cultural connection – from a magical landscape to important historical conservation projects.
properties.verbal_description: The Ottoman Period (1517-1917): In the 13th century, during the Mamluk period, and later in the Ottoman period, there was a significant development in water-powered milling technologies. It is possible that the flour mill was built during these periods, as there is much evidence of similar structures being built in the Land of Israel at that time. The water from Nahal Amal was utilized by canals built around it, and this system allowed for the milling of flour for the local settlements. It is likely that the flour mill was built in the 19th century, during the Ottoman period, and continued to serve the local community for flour milling until the 20th century. After the establishment of the state, the flour mill at Gan HaShlosha (the Sakhne) ceased to be an active agricultural plant, and instead was integrated into conservation efforts as part of the historical heritage of the area. Gan HaShlosha developed into a national resort, with its hot waters and natural pools continuing to attract many visitors. In the 1950s, the site became a major tourist center and it was decided to preserve the mill as part of the open-air museum that presents the agricultural and settlement history of the valley. The uses of the mill gradually became educational and museological, as part of the policy to preserve the Zionist and agricultural heritage in the Beit She'an Valley. With the transition to British rule in the Land of Israel, there was a significant industrial and agricultural development. The Sakhne flour mill moved from active agricultural use to tourist and educational uses. With the establishment of Kibbutz Nir David in 1936, the connection between the Zionist settlement and the utilization of natural water sources for agricultural purposes was strengthened. While the mill gradually fell out of use, it remained part of the local heritage. During the Mandate years, Gan HaShlosha also developed as a recreation area due to its hot springs and unique landscape, and the mill was preserved as part of the historical and agricultural site of the area, in preparation for its use by the general public and for tourism. The Roman-Byzantine Period (1st century to 7th century AD): During this period, the area where the Sakhne is located was part of a large agricultural network that existed throughout the Land of Israel. The state of use of the mill during this period is unknown, but although there is no direct evidence that the current mill was established in the Roman-Byzantine period, irrigation systems, agriculture, and flour mills were common in this period, and it is possible that similar agricultural facilities operated in this area at that time. Roman archaeological finds have been found in the adjacent areas, which suggests the possibility of the presence of an agricultural structure or a similar system that existed at that time.
properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
Physical Condition:

Structure of the Madafa Hall:

Served as a waiting room for customers of the flour mill who came to grind their wheat from the surrounding villages and even from more distant places such as the villages of the Triangle in the drier seasons.

The wait could last from several hours to a few days, during which the customers would rest and talk among themselves. Over the years, the building has undergone renovation and conservation work, its state of preservation is quite good and it is the only building among the central flour mill complex that can still be entered.

Flour Mill Structure:

The building contained two millstone halls, which indicated that this mill was among the most central in the area and had a high water flow and grinding output. In the grinding hall of millstone 1, it operated by means of a system of lifting pools and a chute.

In the grinding hall of millstone 2, it operated by means of a water transport system in channels from the upper natural pool directly into a chimney. Over the years, the central flour mill building has sunk, due to the type of muddy soil it is based on and also because the area where it is located has a high frequency of ground movement, and therefore damage has been created in the form of cracks within the building.

Risks and Sensitivities:

  1. Water and Moisture Damage: The mill is located next to Nahal Amal, which causes hypersensitivity to moisture and erosion of the structure. The stream water can penetrate the foundations of the mill, cause cracks in the stone walls, and damage the original infrastructure, such as the water channels used to drive the grinding wheels. The moisture also creates problems of plant growth and mold on the walls.
  2. Material Weathering: The historical materials of the building (such as stone, plaster, wood, and iron) undergo natural weathering over the years, mainly due to exposure to harsh environmental conditions, such as strong sun, rain, and wind. As a result, damage is caused to the structure of the walls, arches, and water channels, and additional damage to the internal parts of the grinding system.
  3. Earthquakes: The Beit She'an Valley is located in a seismically active area, and the risk of earthquakes could damage the ancient mill, whose stone structure is sensitive to significant ground movements.
  4. Infrastructure Erosion due to Tourist Activity: The national park attracts many tourists every year. The heavy traffic around the mill can cause soil erosion, wear and tear on the paths leading to it, and even damage to the structure, if proper control of visitor movement is not exercised.
  5. Ravages of Time and Neglect: Over the years, historical buildings tend to deteriorate if periodic maintenance work is not carried out on them. Neglect of routine maintenance can lead to cumulative damage.

Conservation Work Carried Out in Light of the Described Risks:

  1. Conservation and Restoration of the Building's Foundations: Restoration and conservation work on the building's foundations was carried out in the 1990s and continued with additional projects in the early 2000s. The work included restoring foundations, walls, and ceilings using original materials such as stone and lime plaster, which were carefully selected to preserve the historical character of the building. Restoration of the building's foundations: This restoration was essential due to damage caused by moisture and natural weathering processes.
  2. Protection against Water and Moisture Damage: Protection against water and moisture damage: Due to the proximity to the stream, it became necessary to protect the building from water damage. In the last decade, between 2010-2020, emphasis was placed on improving the drainage channels to prevent water penetration into the internal areas of the mill. In addition, drying and moisture prevention systems were installed in sensitive corners of the building, especially in areas affected by moisture and mold.
  3. Strengthening the Building against Earthquakes: During the late 2000s, as part of a broad project to strengthen historical buildings in Israel against earthquakes, strengthening work was carried out on the mill using modern technologies. These reinforcements were designed to ensure the stability of the building during an earthquake, while taking care to preserve its original appearance.
  4. Visitor Activity Control: In recent years, as part of the effort to preserve the building from damage resulting from the volume of visitor traffic, marked paths were established and fences were erected around sensitive areas. These projects were carried out during the 2010s, and they include guidance for the general public regarding the importance of preserving the site.
  5. Periodic Maintenance Programs: Since the early 2000s, routine maintenance programs have been developed in cooperation with the Israel Nature and Parks Authority. These programs include regular structural inspections, external and internal cleaning, and immediate repairs of minor damage, in order to ensure the long-term preservation of the site.

These conservation actions were carried out in order to ensure the stability and continuity of the site for future generations, while preserving the original character of the mill.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
The place in its entirety constitutes a significant part of the landscape, and complements the topography; it should be preserved and no destructive/altering actions should be taken that would harm its composition and identity. In terms of its identity and interpretation as a 'mill,' it is recommended to restore the activity of the water channels, and aim for restoration and rehabilitation that allows understanding of the technique by which the mill operated. It is important to preserve all the architectural elements of which the building is composed, and to emphasize its character as a double-penstock mill, where the prominent element was the activity carried out by water power. The elements through which the operation was carried out on two floors, one above the other, should be preserved and restored: the paddle wheel inside the tunnels, the penstock, and the millstone at the level where the grinding takes place. And to address the landscape elements, their placement and the connection between them and the building, to restore and rehabilitate their role and not to change them, such as the connection between the passage - the bridge - and the external stairs leading to each floor, to the stone terraces, and to the intermediary - the orchard - located between them. In addition, to preserve the existing trees in the space.

In general, there should be minimal intervention in the building and no strengthening/burying in concrete. Solutions adapted to the type of stone and the construction method of the building should be found, and broken/insufficiently supported stones should be replaced. Water penetration should be checked on the floors where concrete was used, and they should be rehabilitated. It is recommended to conceal the concrete in the water channel areas, and in the walls and vaults. Sealing work should be carried out at the openings (windows/tile roofs/flat roofs), maintenance work should be carried out on the roofs. And the bridge should be rehabilitated and it should be ensured that the stones are supported and the railing replaced.

1. Conservation and rehabilitation: external stairs, the stone bridge over the Tzippori stream, strengthen the bridge railing, add/repair stones. Doors and windows.

2. Program restoration: removal of internal divisions of spaces and returning them to their former state, as wide and large spaces (on the three levels there are spaces without internal divisions, the situation should be restored to the original as spaces for a flour mill). To restore part of the water channels to operation - requires maintenance. This act can be well integrated with community activities. In preserving the building, the asset can take part in various community activities, and contribute to the whole experience of visitors to the site and the Tzippori stream area. Revitalizing the place with the help of people will perpetuate the mill, especially if it returns to its original function.

In determining the planning boundaries, it was important for us to include the entire mill system – the spring, the aqueduct, and of course the mill with part of the immediate and close environment that surrounds and envelops it.

In conclusion, statutorily, the site area is defined as an open, natural, protected agricultural area. This preserves the natural and original environment of the mill.

As of today, the asset is still owned by the Carmelite Order, but in 2012 it was leased by the Kishon Drainage and Rivers Authority for about 20 years to turn it into a training center for stream rehabilitation. So it is likely that the asset and its entire area are under the responsibility of and managed by the Kishon Drainage and Rivers Authority, which is currently promoting a project for the ecological and environmental rehabilitation of the Tzippori stream in parallel with the conservation and rehabilitation of the Monks' Mill. They also hold various activities and events throughout the year in the vicinity of the mill and the stream.
properties.cultural_assessment_0:
The Monks' Mill in the Tzippori Stream is a double-penstock flour mill that operated using the force of the water current. It is one of a set of mills located along the Tzippori Stream, being among the most developed and largest of them. The mill has existed for over 200 years, owned by the Carmelite Order, hence its name - the Monks' Mill, and in Arabic 'al-Rahib'.

Today, the mill building and other related elements are a prominent part of the cultural landscape unit of the rich and diverse Tzippori Stream, which contains a wide and varied complex of elements related to flour mills and other water reservoirs - the spring pools, the canals, the aqueduct, and the stream. This asset is a living example, still existing in its full glory, of many of the flour mills that were in the country and in the Galilee region in particular. It represents the ancient technology of flour milling that characterizes the period and even shows this method in an unusual complexity and sophistication tailored to the topographical conditions of the wadi.

The story and historical background that brings the building to life and back into operation by the Carmelite Order and the architect-monk from Prascati magnifies, adds to, and enriches the story of the place, preserves it over the years, and dictates its name in parallel with the geopolitical developments of the entire region and especially the strengthening of the churches in the country. The motive for purchasing and renovating the asset was economic gain and a source of income to realize the vision of the Carmelites and rebuild their monastery on the Carmel in Haifa. This adds a religious or cultic value to the mill building. It is important to note that the building had many written testimonies in books and various publications (newspapers) by a variety of witnesses and people, and also documentation in maps and photographs throughout the 19th and 20th centuries.

Likewise, the local building style (local stone and mortar materials) which also incorporates non-local elements (the iron windows and the tiles) stands in good and stable condition and is an architectural gem in nature. Although it was built in different stages, the additions that were made respected what existed before them and were made of the same materials. The interior spaces have an impressive architectural complexity of vaults of different shapes.

The building reflects many values in its construction and existence - the wise and intelligent handling of the existing environment, the use and utilization of ancient technology, and mainly and above all, the development of the settlements around it and the basic need for flour milling. Its function in the area, providing flour to the surrounding settlements, testifies to the connection and dynamics of the former inhabitants with nature, agriculture, water, and food processing, and the fact that it served several settlements at the same time reflects a social, community, and inter-settlement aspect.

We see that through the structure of the mill, one can learn about the connection and respect of the ancient inhabitants of the place for the wadi. And the art they had in leveraging and using natural resources in a harmonious way for man. And therefore, the building itself is authentic and true to the place and the need, and that is what makes it so 'real', local, simple, and integrated. The building makes present and conveys the relationship between man and nature that existed then and it is important that it exists today as well. Therefore, it is essential to preserve, restore, and revive it.

properties.spirit_of_place: The asset is located in a scenic area rich in the Tzippori Stream route. It is built of local stone and is situated within the existing topography, mediating between the steep hill and the stream, surrounded by pastoral and green nature, far from urban developments, and in a quiet and serene environment. Its natural surroundings are relatively open and wide, with diverse vegetation accompanying it. The building stands and overlooks in a stable and firm manner as if it has always been there. It is clear that the building is made of different parts, each part built of a different material at a different stage. This variety of structures gives it a timeless feel, as if it has been standing there for a long time and is still in use today.
properties.description:
The Monks' Mill, in Arabic 'Tahunat al-Rahib', is a building from the Ottoman period that existed even before 1821. The building was built and developed in stages, and at each stage, it was part of a different story that passed it on to its next incarnation. Today, the building is a terraced structure with 4 levels, adjacent to a slope - a double-penstock mill building.

The asset is situated on the northern bank of the Tzippori Stream, and it is part of the landscape unit of the lower Tzippori Stream. The stream's surroundings are an area with fertile soil and proximity to water sources; these conditions encouraged settlement from ancient times. Likewise, the stream's route was a passage between two major cities at the time - Acre and Nazareth. This strategic and rich route is the background, basis, and environmental framework in which the mill was established.

The exact date and circumstances of the mill's establishment are unknown to us, but it was likely built by a Druze family from one of the nearby villages, Shefa-'Amr, to serve the city and the settlements in its vicinity and supply them with flour, such as - Majdal, Tzippori, and Tivon. Around the year 1821, the mill ceased to operate. If we follow the historical maps of the area, on Jaction's map of 1799, the mill is not marked, which may indicate that it was already abandoned by then until the Carmelites arrive and receive it in a condition they reported as abandoned and neglected. In 1819, a Carmelite monk named Giambattista from Prascati, an architect by training, arrived in the country on behalf of the Carmelite Order to renovate the Carmelite monastery in Haifa after it had been destroyed twice - in 1761 by Dhaher al-Omar and in 1821 by Abdullah Pasha. Upon his arrival, the Carmelite monk from Prascati sought a source of income to carry out the renovation of the monastery, and he remembered the existing mills halfway between Acre and Nazareth. He approached a wealthy Turkish man and together they renewed the mill's operation while developing and improving it. This step helped the Carmelites to fully finance the renovation and complete the monastery that exists to this day in Haifa. This story is directly and closely linked to the mill, and as a result, its name was coined - the Monks' Mill (in Arabic 'Tahunat al-Rahib'). The mills ceased to operate around 1930, due to the establishment of electric mills in Shefa-'Amr and Ibtin, or due to a lack of water in the stream. At this point, the mill reached the end of its function as a flour mill.

Around the 1950s, the building served as a shelter for the local flocks and even as a pigsty. Later, in the 2000s, it underwent renovation and served as an event hall, a restaurant, and guest rooms. This business closed, and from 2012 to the present, it has been under the responsibility of the Kishon Drainage and Rivers Authority to turn it into a training center for stream rehabilitation. Today (2024), the building is a structure standing in the heart of the Tzippori Stream valley, and it is part of the amazing landscape unit of the area. The asset is visible from afar, standing whole and stable with its four levels, the bridge, and the orchard.

There is information about the asset, with much of the material concentrated in a comprehensive documentation file titled 'Tzippori Stream - The Monks' Mill' prepared by Ruth Liberty-Shalev and commissioned by the Kishon Drainage and Rivers Authority in 2012. This documentation file also contained earlier information and references, so most of the information we will use for our work was from this last documentation file.

The mill asset was established in the Ottoman period and operated until the beginning of the 20th century. It is likely that in the early history of the mill, the flour milling operation relied on the flow of water in the stream. Later, the mill was expanded and a built aqueduct was developed, which transferred the water from the spring to the penstocks at the upper level of the mill, and the force of the falling water drove the millstones that ground the flour.
The assumption, based on the existing data at the site, is that the mill was built in stages that indicate its development in different periods. In the first stage, which is very speculative and lacks documented facts, the sources assume that the mill included a single stone building located near the stream's course and relied on the power of the stream's current for flour milling. The building included two levels: a lower level of two tunnels 2m high that included the paddle wheel that was once active and rotated by water pressure, and an upper level with two vaulted ceilings 4.10m high that included the mill. Assuming this was the first stage of the building, the following stages came after it:
In the second stage, another stone level was added to the mill, adjacent to the first level in a terraced manner, which may have served to support the aqueducts, so that the building consisted of one level of a mill that included the two millstones, and below it tunnels, and a secondary building. The mill became a penstock mill, whose water source was the water that flowed from the Tzippori Stream to the upper part of the secondary building.
In the third stage, the upper mills were added to the mill. The assumption is that this action was done during the Carmelite period. It can be assumed that they intervened in the first mill on the lower level and renovated the facades of the building. And then continued the construction while respecting the existing material and the existing environment. During this period, a built aqueduct was developed that transferred the water from the spring as a new water source (Ras al-Ain spring) to the penstocks at the upper level of the mill and by the force of the falling water, the millstones that ground the flour were driven. The water that came from the new upper part was poured into the previous channel. After the mills stopped operating, around the 1930s, the mill underwent renovation and a change was made to the windows. Iron was used as an element for framing the windows, coinciding with the beginning of the use of iron in the construction industry worldwide. This means that the windows were brought from abroad, and this was an unprecedented step in the use of non-local elements and materials. The bridge located over the Tzippori Stream leading to the building was also renovated.

properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
Substantial changes in program and use - internal divisions in the mill spaces, which are built as a typical mill space, change the purpose of these spaces and damage the original program.

Blocking access and closing openings - blocking access to the lower wheel tunnels on the southern facade by building a stone wall (it is not known when or for what purpose), which prevents access and assessment of the condition of the tunnels.

Irreversible damage to the restoration of the water penstocks - a later concrete addition that causes damage to the building and does not preserve it, the addition of concrete floors in places where there is a water system that would be better to restore.

Renovation of the facades - facades were renovated in the 1820s.

According to the engineering report, it is written that the building is generally stable, in some of the facades and walls the mortar has been washed away and the stones have been significantly eroded by weathering, and in the internal vaults there is very high humidity. These things could endanger the stability of the building. The roofs are also in poor condition and some have been damaged by rot. The bridge leading to the mill is completely stable.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations: Mill M9 has great archaeological importance, and its conservation and development as a visitor attraction should be recommended. It is recommended to establish a visitor center in the mill's space, where illustrations of the development of the mill enterprise and the various water technologies will be displayed. The establishment of the center will require the full restoration of the building, including an archaeological excavation to locate ancient remains. In addition, there is a need to expose the original water routes and allow for the controlled and orderly flow of water, without harming the preservation of the remains. The conservation of the mill buildings will require cleaning, exposure, stabilization, and completion of missing stones, along with the renewal of pointing and plaster. It is also recommended to restore some of the mill's facilities, such as the wheel at mill M10, to display the traditional technology. Restoring the flowing water to the area will help demonstrate the historical connections between the mills and the stream and the nature reserve, and will enhance the visitor experience. All these actions can contribute to the preservation of cultural heritage and strengthen the connection between visitors and this unique site. As part of the conservation and demonstration of the row of mills, it is recommended to work to flow water through most of the facilities to demonstrate the technology and to enhance the experience of visiting the reserve. The recommended planning boundary encloses the area of mill M9, the diversion dam, and mills M10-M13 for the purpose of demonstrating the proposed mill route.
properties.management_data_notes: The Nahal Amud Reserve is one of the first reserves declared by the State of Israel. The reserve is managed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority. The reserve enjoys broad legal protection, including recognition as an antiquities site and detailed planning in the area. The statutory protection is intended to preserve the values of nature, landscape, and historical heritage in the area. Alongside the legal protection, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, together with the Israel Antiquities Authority, carry out routine management activities, such as supervision, maintenance, and infrastructure development, to maintain the quality of the environment and ensure a pleasant visiting experience for hikers. The degree of supervision and maintenance varies between different areas in the reserve, with a daily presence of inspectors in the touristed areas, while in more remote areas the supervision may be less frequent.
properties.cultural_assessment_0:
The Batan fulling mill in Nahal Amud is located at a strategic point between Nahal Meron and Nahal Amud, on the slopes of the Eastern Galilee mountains. The stream receives its water from various springs in the area, including Ein Seter and Ein Yakim, and drains the southern slopes of the Meron mountains towards the Sea of Galilee. The annual flow of the stream, which was essential for the operation of the mills throughout the year, directly affected their function, especially during the winter and spring when water flowed abundantly. Along 2.5 km of the upper stream, there are 18 flour mills, with the Batan mill being the most prominent. The mill was built in the Crusader period on earlier foundations, and was originally used for grinding flour for the local population in Safed. In the 16th century, a large immigration of Jews of Spanish origin arrived in Safed. In the 14th-15th centuries, the wool industry developed in Spain. The demand for woolen fabrics provided a livelihood for a third of the population of the Castile region and was the primary source of income for the Jews of Spain. With the expulsion of the Jews from Spain, they sought a new source of livelihood. Thessaloniki, being a port city, met their requirements as it was a crossroads where high-quality wool could be obtained. The military and civil apparatus of the Ottoman government, which demanded high-quality clothing, were a promising customer base. After the conquest of the country by the Turks, the longing of the exiles to settle it and probably also the abundance of professionals in Thessaloniki led to the development of a woolen fabric industry in Safed, whose natural conditions were suitable for production needs. The exiles brought their knowledge with them and preserved the name of the fulling mill in Spanish: Batan. In the Hebrew literature of the period, these fulling mills are mentioned in several sources: Joseph Karo in his responsa (..full quote), Hayyim Vital in Sha'ar HaGilgulim mentions in the grave markings around Safed that: 'Below the mountain there is one Batan where they prepare the clothes, and it is the largest Batan in that river,' and other mentions.

The activity in the wool industry in the stream reached its peak in the 16th century, when S. Avitzur, estimating the amount of fabrics produced from the tax data and the required process, estimates that about 6 of the stream's mills were converted into fulling mills during the 16th century, with the number of hammers in them varying from 2 to 6 hammers per mill depending on the strength of the flow, which weakens as one gets further from the source of the spring.

After the decline of the wool industry due to difficulty in obtaining raw materials and changes in the Turkish government that led to restrictions and taxation that made it difficult to purchase raw wool and transport it, so that the final price was so expensive that it was not worthwhile to produce. The settlement, which had lost its main source of livelihood, gradually dwindled. Until the 1670s, simple wool products were produced from local wool, about a fifth of the previous production volume. (according to S. Avitzur)

With the decline in the need for fulling, the fulling mills were converted to flour mills, as evidenced by the remains found in the stream, all of which are of flour mills. However, it is almost certain that most of the mills were built on earlier remains and it is possible that some of them were fulling mills.
Mill 9M, adjacent to the south of the confluence of the Meron and Amud streams, is known to all as the 'Fulling Mill'. Although its interior space is relatively large, and its construction is particularly massive, the remains of the facilities are those of a flour mill. Its name derives from its Arabic name, which probably preserved its original purpose - 'Tahunat al-Batan', 'batan' in Spanish means fulling mill. Remains of earlier facilities that may have been used for the fulling process are located near mill 14M downstream (see Chapter 5 - Documentation of Existing Condition). In any case, it is clear that from the 17th century until the establishment of the state, flour mills operated in Nahal Amud.

The use of the mill finally ceased at the beginning of the 20th century with the installation of concrete aqueducts along the entire row of mills. These aqueducts replaced the aqueducts built of stone and the channels dug in the natural ground, so that the construction of the concrete aqueducts significantly improved the system's watertightness and efficiency. In places where there were large slopes to bridge, iron pipes and pits were installed. Every few mills, additional channels were added to increase the flow of water to the system by means of diversion dams.

While the system was being improved, there was also a significant decrease in the demand for flour milling in the stream, as engine-powered mills began to develop in Safed and grain merchants began to sell ready-made flour in the city. The mills continued to operate mainly for the needs of the fellahin wheat owners, and with the departure of the Arab population from the city at the end of the War of Independence, the mills ceased to operate.

The condition of the mill today is reflected in extensive documentation work done during the 1980s by Emmanuel Damati, and according to the documentation survey of the architects Amir Freundlich and Yaara Shaltiel, who conducted a broad documentation survey of the flour mills in Nahal Amud, including mill M9 - the Fulling Mill. According to the documentation file, it appears that the last intervention made in the building was in the 1990s and in 2014, when the action taken was mainly pruning of vegetation. The mill building is the most stable and complete building among all the flour mills in Nahal Amud, with its activity having ceased at the beginning of the 20th century, as the concrete channel attests - blocking the water outlet.

The flour mills and fulling mills along the stream, including the Batan mill, are an example of the successful combination of utilizing natural resources for a thriving agricultural industry. Their location in the Nahal Amud reserve, among tall plane trees and rich stream vegetation, adds landscape and cultural value to the place and attracts many hikers throughout the year. The paths surrounding the site, including the Israel National Trail, connect the Batan mill to the other mills, and constitute a historical-cultural route that exposes hikers to the industrial history of the area.

properties.spirit_of_place:
The documentation file by architects Amir Freundlich and Yaara Shaltiel paints a rich and detailed picture of the flour mills and the fulling mill in Nahal Amud, allowing us to experience the unique 'spirit of the place'. Based on photographs, sketches, and detailed descriptions, we experience a journey back in time to an era when water was the engine of life and stone was the foundation of every structure.

During a visit to the flour mills and the fulling mill in Nahal Amud, the feeling of the 'spirit of the place' reveals the wonderful combination of nature and history into a deep and unique experience. Upon arriving at the site, the disconnection from the modern world is realized through the silence that accompanies the flowing water. The sound of the water in Nahal Amud conveys a sense of calm and emphasizes the natural disconnection from the surrounding technological world, and recalls days when the simple power of water was the main engine for the economy and daily work. The high cliffs surrounding the stream, the wide plane trees, and the green environment create a feeling of wild and untouched nature.

The ancient flour mills are built of local stones that blend naturally and archaically into the landscape, giving a sense of ancient power in which man worked in cooperation with the environment. The deep history of the place is felt in every corner, as every step on the ground evokes thoughts of generations of residents who lived in the place, ground grain, and processed wool in the nearby fulling mill. The feeling of life dependent on the stream and the flow of water runs like a thread through every visit, and the experience is one of a deep connection to nature and history that still breathes its presence in the place.

The encounter with the sounds, smells, and landscape enhances the feeling of connection to a place where time seems to stand still. The flour mills and the fulling mill, although no longer active, exude a quiet and deep presence that inspires admiration and appreciation for the simple yet content-rich past.

properties.mapping_description: The Batan mill in Nahal Amud is located in the upper part of the stream, near Safed and Meron, and is part of a complex system of flour mills that were powered by water. The site also has remains of diversion dams and bridges that were used to direct the flow of water. The area of mill M9 - the Batan mill is enclosed in a polygon on the map, with the point to the right of the building indicating the remnant of the bridge that led to it, and the point to the left representing the diversion dam that was used to divert water towards the mill. The historical roads that led to the mill are marked with a line on the map, connecting the mill with the nearby settlements, as they once served as main traffic arteries for the residents of the area and the workers in the mills.

properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
According to the documentation survey, in the early 1920s, part of the fulling mill building collapsed, mainly in the front of the building. Following the collapse, fundamental restoration work was carried out on the building, which included reconstruction and repair of the facade using only natural materials. The materials used were local stone and wood, in order to preserve the authenticity of the building and adapt it to the natural environment in which it is located. The restoration process was intended to restore the building in appearance and function as close as possible to its original condition.

Despite the collapse and the need for restoration, the Batan mill is the most stable and complete building among all the mills scattered along the stream. The building has survived in relatively good condition, and it continues to serve as an example of the use of traditional technologies for harnessing water power for local industrial purposes. The last intervention made in the building was in 2014, and it included only light pruning of the vegetation surrounding the building, without changing its physical condition.

The flour mill went out of use at the beginning of the 20th century, as evidenced by the concrete channel at its foot, which blocked the water outlet. It is not possible to understand unequivocally what the source of the water that supplied its power was – it may have come from the nearby orchard or from the salamander pool, and perhaps also from the Meron mills. Over the years, it is possible that a variety of sources were used simultaneously. The building continues to stand to this day as a living testimony to the industrial and agricultural activity that took place in the area for hundreds of years.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
Conservation Recommendations:

Critical evaluation of the conservation project or interventions already carried out, or the uses of the site:

  • Agreement of all stakeholders to proceed with the implementation stages – absolute majority approach: The planning process for the dam's rehabilitation turned from a conflict between the various stakeholders into a process of full cooperation. This made it possible to implement the planning of a complex engineering project in a sensitive manner within a nature reserve. The cooperation was created after the archaeological excavation revealed the dam's unique engineering qualities. The engineering solutions were chosen jointly, with an approach requiring the agreement of all stakeholders to proceed with the implementation stages ('absolute majority rules'). The members of the planning team and the steering committee almost all mention the professional and respectful nature of the discussion led by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority and the harmony between the team members.
  • Importance of the social aspect – integration of the nearby settlement of Jisr az-Zarqa into the project: The project management team members emphasized the importance of integrating the residents of the nearby settlement. They were asked to create a system of involved residents who take part in various activities in the reserve and show care for the condition and integrity of the site.
  • Possibility of using ancient facilities and water operators for engineering use at present and future flows: The Nahal Taninim dam project is a precedent for a conservation project that is active in the original way it operated in the past. The dam is not only an exceptional travel experience for the visiting public, making use of meticulous restoration and conservation to display historical assets, but also an engineering solution to a drainage problem, based on historical infrastructure existing at the site.
  • Integration of the Taninim Dam and the reserve as an organic part of the landscape of the Kabara Valley and the landscape of the stream's estuary: The Taninim Dam is a local and regional site that tells the multi-dimensional historical story of the basin's landscape. Today, the historical story is partially realized at the reserve site. Several stakeholders have made proposals to promote new projects in the area: for example, creating a spatial link between existing and planned projects in the area, such as the fishing village in Jisr az-Zarqa and a bird-watching park in Ma'agan Michael.

Recommendations for planning and conservation principles:

  1. Maintenance:

Integration of neighboring communities in the area's activities: Findings from the site, currently displayed at the Ma'agan Michael Museum, can be integrated as part of a comprehensive tour for visitors to the complex, or these items can be borrowed from the exhibition. In addition, integrating the population of the neighboring settlements, through the integration of students and youth movements in the development and operation of message tourism and employment projects, near the complex. While emphasizing giving a special status to the populations of the neighboring settlements who in the past enjoyed free access to the complex, in order to give them a sense of belonging to the 'renewed' site.

  1. Monitoring:

Monitoring is currently being carried out at the site: treatment of invasive species, fish monitoring, and water resource management at the site according to the different needs in the reservoir, in the pool downstream of the dam, and in the facilities. We recommend continuing these actions, which are of great importance in preserving the asset and the site's environment, which is an integral part of the experience there.

  1. Conservation and Rehabilitation:
  • Restoration of the original arch in the Ottoman flour mill, which was restored in an inauthentic way (a round arch instead of a pointed one).
  • The site adjacent to the Nahal Taninim complex, the 'Aqueduct in Beit Hanania', has not undergone conservation despite the site being worthy and in need of it. We recommend carrying out a conservation process at this asset, with an emphasis on 'linking the asset' to the neighboring Nahal Taninim complex (through signage from Highway 2, a hiking trail, and shuttles between the two assets - to create a complete travel experience).
  • Planning of an artificial body of water north of the existing lifting pool – in the area enclosed between Nahal Ada and Nahal Taninim.
  1. Hazard Removal:
  • Raising, widening, or diverting Highway 2 to reduce the chance of flooding of the Nahal Taninim complex and the flour mills.
  • Expanding the asset's boundaries: The dam, the pool, and the flour mills are part of a wide complex of assets that were part of the project of bringing water to ancient Caesarea. The asset's area does not end at Highway 2 to the west, and at the nearby settlements to its north and south. It is part of a wider complex. The complex of assets can be linked together by creating a vehicle route that passes between these points and tells the story of the water transport to Caesarea in installments. This route is significant not only for understanding the complete historical story of the site, but also for preserving and raising awareness of the need to preserve all these assets, among which are sites such as the aqueduct in Beit Hanania that have not received basic protection.

Recommendation for planning boundaries:

The Nahal Taninim National Park contains findings that are part of a broader picture, telling the story of the water transport to Caesarea in the Byzantine period. This story unfolds over a wide variety of sites in the country, including: the ancient city of Caesarea, Shuni, the aqueduct in Beit Hanania, and more, in a way that sheds light on the way of life of the residents of ancient Caesarea in the Byzantine period. For this reason, we believe that the existing boundaries of the site (within its fence), between Highway 2, and the settlements to its north and south, 'imprison' the space and create the illusion that it stands alone, when it is only part of a larger picture. In order to connect the site to the broader picture, we believe that the site should be treated as part of the complete water transport axis, and a physical way should be found to make these connections present and to expand the park complex.

properties.management_data_notes:
The Nahal Taninim flour mill complex is managed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, and is defined in the master plan as a national park and nature reserve.

  1. Statutory Protection:

According to the master plan, the site is on two adjacent plots: one, a national park, and the other, a nature reserve. According to Israeli law, a national park is a park defined as an area for recreation or commemoration of archaeological, historical, or architectural value. The park will be managed by a body chosen by the Knesset for this purpose; this body will act to protect the site's area, is entitled to charge an entrance fee, and to appoint supervision on its behalf. A nature reserve is an area where fauna, flora, and inanimate objects of scientific and educational importance are located, which has been declared a national site. It is forbidden to cause damage to this area; a permit is granted for management by a non-profit corporation that will hold, care for, operate, and cultivate the site. A body can be appointed to supervise the site, and an entrance fee can be charged. (From the National Parks, Nature Reserves, National Sites and Memorial Sites Law, 5758-1998)

  1. Management Actions:

The Nahal Taninim Reserve is managed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority. A team of the Authority's employees is in charge of the site, who work to manage the entrance to the site and collect the entrance fee, maintain the infrastructure, and protect the site's assets.

Cultural Assessment

Based on the Burra Charter and a review of the site as a whole, we believe that the project embodies many values, including historical value, which is expressed in the fact that the site is a living testimony to 1,600 years of hydraulic history. It also has scientific-archaeological value, as the site is a unique archaeological find in Israel. It includes a variety of structures from various historical periods that have been exceptionally well preserved, a wide collection of flour mills from various periods, a large number of mills preserved in the same area, and a display of milling technologies that exist only at this site (horizontal paddle wheel). In addition to these, we believe that the site embodies values of nature, landscape, and ecology, as the complex includes two streams, a dam, and unique local vegetation and plant species. Together with the impressive collection of architectural monuments, this creates a unique sensory experience and a breathtaking aesthetic experience, which attest to the existence of these two values (aesthetics and sensory experience). It is important to note that the national park is of great importance as a space where the neighboring communities, from Jisr az-Zarqa and Kibbutz Ma'agan Michael, meet. Therefore, the site embodies a social value. Furthermore, the fact that the site has preserved findings of hydraulic technology systems, which shed light on the historical development of flour mills in the Land of Israel, from the Byzantine mills with the vertical paddle wheel, through the penstock mills from the Crusader period, to their conversion to chute mills with the lowering of the water in the dam during the Ottoman period and the construction of the horizontal paddle wheels, attests to the site's scientific value. It is important to note that the state of preservation of the monuments at the site allows for viewing a wide range of monuments that have been preserved in high quality, clearly demonstrating their original purpose and allowing for a comprehensive view of the complete story of the space. In a way that is unparalleled in Israel and the world, which emphasizes the rarity value of the space, where there are a wide variety of flour mills that display, in a well-preserved manner, milling technologies from various different periods unique to the Land of Israel. Its monuments have not only value in themselves but are also part of a fabric and complex that tells the story of the water transport to Caesarea in the Byzantine period. This story unfolds over a wide variety of sites in the country, from the Shuni amphitheater through the aqueduct in Beit Hanania to Caesarea itself, and is currently a unique representation of its kind in Israel and the world, demonstrating in a 'living' way unique findings from a variety of historical periods, including the Byzantine period, the Crusader period, and the Ottoman period. Each of these is worthy of conservation in its own right as it is a well-preserved item (almost complete) that clearly demonstrates the way of life of this historical period in the Land of Israel, demonstrating the importance of the site as a tool for reflecting many historical periods, in which findings were documented. In unique excavations in Israel and the world, including the horizontal milling paddle wheels from the Ottoman period.

Examination of Authenticity and Completeness:

Based on the Nara Document on Authenticity, we believe that the historical evidence reflected in the variety of findings found at the Nahal Taninim National Park reflects the broad story of the site and the transformations it has undergone over 1,600 years. The findings at the national park have been preserved in high quality, reflecting all the historical layers that the space has undergone. Both in the way the findings have been preserved at the site in relation to their original location, alongside the reservoir, the dam, and the aqueducts, in a way that demonstrates the complete story of the history of milling at the site and the use of hydraulic technologies for milling. And in the way the space demonstrates its many connections to its wider surroundings. As the site is part of the story of the water transport to Caesarea in the Byzantine period. This story unfolds over a wide variety of sites in the country, including: the ancient city of Caesarea, Shuni, the aqueduct in Beit Hanania, and more. This environment is also significant in the landscape sense, as the site is part of a wide landscape environment, and includes the Ada and Taninim streams, the water reservoir, and alongside them the historical buildings: the dam and the flour mills, whose operation was based on the existence of this landscape environment. The presentation of these findings within the landscape environment that served their existence attests to the unique character of the place and the findings found there, which are located within the geographical, physical, and historical context of their development. The design of the space allows a glimpse into the original milling processes, in their original location and with the original materials and technology of the space. As the paddle wheels have been preserved in their original form (or restored based on original findings), and have been placed in a way that demonstrates the historical construction and operation methods in the space. It can be said that the site authentically demonstrates the construction history of the ancient periods, and thus preserves the spirit of the place. The Nahal Taninim Reserve is a pastoral space and a green gem, located between the foothills of the Carmel and the sea. This space provides a historical and sensory experience, where the visitor experiences history firsthand, and sees the flour mills operating for their original purpose, at their original geographical location, in a way that provides a complete experience of the historical story of the water transport and milling system in the area. It is important to note that despite the authenticity of the space, mistakes were made in the restoration of the arch in the northern (Ottoman) flour mill, which was restored in a way that does not match the original as was later revealed from photographs that were found, which indicates that despite the high-quality conservation work in the space, the site is not 100% authentic.

Spirit of the Place - Sensory Description

The Nahal Taninim Nature Reserve is a pastoral space and a green gem, nestled between the foothills of the Carmel and the sea. This space provides a historical and sensory experience, where the visitor experiences history firsthand, seeing the historic watermills in operation for their original purpose, the dam opening to the sound of rushing water, in an environment rich with local flora and fauna. Apart from the absent crocodiles, it is an authentic experience of a journey through the pages of history. In addition to being a pastoral space, the reserve is rich in vegetation and wildlife. Alongside the Taninim reservoir, the sea, and a host of historic flour mill buildings, there is a wealth of plant and animal species. The nature reserve offers a glimpse into a unique local ecosystem that has developed in this area, with a variety of animals such as soft-shelled turtles, pond turtles, river crabs, toads, octopuses, jungle cats, mongooses, herons, and kingfishers. Vegetation includes tamarisks, holy bramble, sugarcane, crocus, squill, and lotus. Furthermore, the reserve contains several unique monuments. Among them is the dam structure: this massive structure, spanning over 194 m in length and standing about 7 m high, has been preserved in high quality, so that its original grandeur and historical purpose can still be witnessed. In addition to the dam structure, the reserve contains a variety of flour mills and buildings from different historical periods, from the Byzantine flour mills to the Ottoman mill. The buildings at the site display an architectural and visual richness, demonstrating the multi-layered history that has left its mark on the site's structures, through typological and morphological complexity, making the Nahal Taninim complex unique in Israel and the world. It has preserved a variety of flour mills and hydraulic milling technologies from various periods in the history of the Land of Israel. These technologies are also unique in the world, and exceptional in the quality of their preservation. The entire complex provides a glimpse into a complete historical story, spanning 1,600 years of construction and dismantling, representing the multi-generational nature of the site and the region. The uniqueness of the site is not only summed up in the wealth of findings within its territory, but also in the fact that the site still serves today as a means of flood drainage and as an active national park, thus continuing the tradition of its original purpose and serving as a living testimony to ancient technology that is relevant even today. The space also serves as a meeting place for the two neighboring communities - Ma'agan Michael and Jisr az-Zarqa, allowing the residents of the area to connect with each other through the shared historical space.

properties.description:
The Nahal Taninim flour mill complex is located in the 'Nahal Taninim' nature reserve between Ma'agan Michael and Jisr az-Zarqa, in the Hof HaCarmel Regional Council. The Nahal Taninim reserve covers an area of 470 dunams. Along the two western kilometers of the stream lie the Nahal Taninim dam and its mills. These are part of an engineering complex that transported water through the low aqueduct to Caesarea. The low aqueduct to Caesarea was built in the Byzantine period and joined a series of existing aqueducts that transported water from Shuni, through Beit Hanania, to Caesarea. Together, these created an impressive historical complex of sites that tell the story of the water supply to Caesarea in a unique and complete way. The Nahal Taninim National Park, in particular, is currently a unique representation of its kind in Israel and the world, demonstrating in a 'living' way the history of the flour mills and the dam at the site. The site has undergone an in-depth conservation process and excavations. On a tour of it, one can see a variety of active flour mills and a host of historical layers that give the site its typological and morphological richness. The periods of activity at the site, including the Byzantine period, the Crusader period, and the Ottoman period, have left their physical mark on it, in the form of building additions to the flour mills, and technological additions to the milling methods. These can be seen, thanks to the thorough conservation, documentation, and excavation work, managed in a joint operation by the Israel Antiquities Authority, Mei Carmel, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, and regional councils, which have turned this archaeological site into a living and active national park that displays the various structures at the site in an almost complete form, demonstrating and actually practicing the ancient tradition. In addition, the site embodies values of nature, landscape, and ecology, which are expressed in the existence of two streams, a dam, and many species of unique local flora and fauna, including soft-shelled turtles, pond turtles, river crabs, toads, octopuses, jungle cats, mongooses, herons, and kingfishers. Vegetation includes tamarisks, holy bramble, sugarcane, crocus, squill, and lotus.

Periods and Uses:

The development process of the flour mills at Nahal Taninim consisted of several stages:
A. The Byzantine Period: 324-638

The Byzantine Period - Roman Dam
• Construction of the dam
• Water regulation facility
• Carving of the 6 Byzantine flour mills in proximity to the dam.
• The operating mechanism includes a vertical wheel, two chutes, two pairs of millstones, and a common grinding floor.

The Roman dam was the basis of a sophisticated water project, designed to raise the water level of Nahal Taninim so that it could be flowed by gravity to Caesarea, the largest city in the Land of Israel at the time. The dam is a huge stone wall – 194 m long and 4 m wide at the top and 10 m wide at the base. The width of the dam is not uniform because supports were added to it over the years.
2. The Byzantine Period - Water Regulation Facility:
The heart of the dam is the regulation facility. Liftable wooden doors released water from the lake to an aqueduct to Caesarea. A high aqueduct, older than it, flowed drinking-quality water from the upper springs of Nahal Taninim in Shuni (near Amikam). The wooden doors of the dam have been restored, and by lifting them, water can be released from the lake. The full restoration of an ancient dam to recreate a lake is one of the wonders of the site, perhaps unique in the world.

The Byzantine Period - The Ancient Mills:
• Location: The ancient mill was built on the existing dam.
• Structure: The mill in the dam consists of a vertical wheel, two chutes, and two pairs of millstones, and it has two levels: a lower level called the drive floor, whose function is to drive the water to the paddle wheels, and above it a grinding floor that has not been preserved. Based on the building remains, it can be inferred that the grinding floor was a common elongated vault for both units together.
• Time of mill operation: The quality of the mill's construction indicates that it was built after the dam was erected and was not planned in advance during its construction. Its main parts were attached to the dam and are not integrated into it. It is difficult to know the date of the mill's construction, but it can be roughly estimated that it was built 100-200 years after the construction of the dam.
B. The Crusader Period: 1099-1187
• 'Repair'
• A blockage in the Byzantine channel, creation of a new mill consisting of a vertical wheel and one chute with undershot operation - which drove one millstone.

Location: The Crusader mill was built on top of the Byzantine mill.
• Structure: After one channel in the Byzantine mechanism was blocked, a new mill was created consisting of a vertical wheel and one chute with undershot operation that operated one millstone. In the eastern wall of the channel, there is a built 'window' connecting it to a room with a concrete cast floor where a mechanism for reversing the mill's operating axis was installed.
• Time of mill operation: The assessment based on the excavations is that the mill was built in the Crusader period according to technological principles known in Europe. It seems that the mill ceased to function after the abandonment of the area following a deliberate policy of the Mamluks to prevent settlement on the coast and in the Caesarea area.
C. The Ottoman Period: 1516-1917
• Construction of the Ottoman flour mill – the most technological.
• The mill is built with a horizontal wheel, a chute or a penstock, a grinding floor, and next to it another room intended for storing the grains before grinding.
• The technology developed by the Ottomans allows for greater control over the amount of water exiting the chute.

Location: The later mill is located in the northwestern part of the dam.
• Structure: It operates in the form of a horizontal wheel and one penstock or chute. To re-qualify the mill, it was necessary to deepen the channel and narrow it on the northern side to control the water flow. The new grinding floor that was built was smaller than its predecessor and a rectangular room was added to it, probably for storing grains before grinding.
• Time of mill operation: Pottery shards from the Ottoman period were found in the excavations in the various components of the mill.

From 1924, the reserve stood abandoned until 1997, when archaeological excavations began following floods in the area, at the initiative of the Mei Carmel organization to deal with the dam at the site. This decision later initiated the beginning of the conservation process of the dam and the mills. It is important to note that the site was declared a nature reserve in 1972, despite this declaration, the conservation process only began in 2000 and was completed in 2009.
