properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
Environmental Hazard (natural wear of material, decay, etc.):

  • Rescue plaster on the junction of the reservoir with the dam structure – plastering a protective layer of hydraulic plaster along the entire flooded section above the original plaster to seal the dam against water seepage.

  • Rehabilitation of the original hydraulic plaster layer, below the water level in the dam structure - with the excavations around the dam, sections of the original hydraulic plaster were exposed that required immediate treatment to prevent its separation from the dam stones. The treatment included stabilizing the edges of the plaster, washing the voids, and filling them with a special material.

  • Reconstruction of the original paddle wheels - in order to reuse the mills, as the original paddle wheels were in a state of decay, which required protecting them from daily operation.

  • Reservoir ecological monitoring activities - treatment of invasive species, fish monitoring, and water resource management at the site according to the various needs in the reservoir, in the pool downstream of the dam, and in the facilities.

  • Stabilization of Ottoman feeding channels: The stones around these channels were subject to extreme erosion, damage, and decay, and needed to be treated to stop the spread of the processes; the treatment involved filling voids and joints with grout, replacing missing stones, and re-plastering.

Man-made Hazard (vandalism):

  • Fencing the complex, ticketed entrance, inspectors.

Environmental Hazard (collapse, falling from winds, collapse - due to ground movement, flooding due to precipitation, etc.):

  • Breaching the dam - the aspiration of the drainage bodies involved in the planning process to prevent flooding on Highway 2 and in the neighboring settlements required breaching the dam over a width of more than 20 m, which was considered unreasonable given the historical and archaeological importance of the monument. Several alternatives were examined, and eventually, it was agreed to excavate the southern part of the dam to determine the location of the dam's original outlets, which would provide increased flow. The pit was then excavated to its full depth, including the three passages, the distribution basin, and the western outlet. In addition, the shutters of the regulation facility were reconstructed. It should be noted that raising the shutters in case of fear of flooding is the responsibility of the reserve manager.

  • The dam as a bridge – The dam has always served as a pedestrian bridge. Parts of the paving stones from the Ottoman period have even been preserved. However, there were sunken areas, and for the safety of visitors, it was decided to replace the missing paving with permeable surfaces and to lay surfaces along the dam. Therefore, packed sub-base layers were installed along the entire length.

  • All exposed components of the dam, treatment for stabilization purposes: Replacing the mortar and filling the core in the joints between the building stones to seal the wall against water and prevent the loss of the original core.

  • Stabilization of the passage from the distribution basin to the channel - in the southern wall of the distribution basin, a carved window was found through which water was flowed from the basin to the aqueduct. The flow of water over the years eroded the rock and left a rocky stump in which cracks formed that endangered its stability. Due to the importance of the original rock, an external steel support was installed to secure it.

Critical Assessment

Advantages:

The project helped preserve the site's heritage and allows for an acquaintance with the history of the place and the traditional milling process.

The complex serves as an educational center that holds workshops and activities related to flour milling and the ancient use of the building in its technological and social aspects.

The rehabilitation of the public space and its access routes has made the site area a pleasant and quiet area with easy access.

Disadvantages:

Concern about further developments in the area.

The site and its surroundings require many and continuous maintenance operations.

Over-development and intervention may cause the site to lose the authenticity and charm it once had for society and users.

Uses on site:

An educational center that includes workshops, activities, and tours that make the history and technology of the place accessible to the public.

A pleasant and quiet leisure area that includes walking paths and areas for lounging and picnics.

The conservation at the 7 Mills flour mill is an excellent example of an effort to preserve local heritage, but it is necessary to maintain a balance between preserving history and modern development, to ensure that the site continues to serve as an educational and community center. Routine maintenance, along with a clear plan to prevent harmful developments, are critical to the success of the building. It is important to note that there is a fine line between conservation that is right for the place and a conservation action that fails to convey the spirit of the place that once prevailed there, and therefore this specific place in this specific location requires meticulous and considerate treatment.

Recommendations for planning principles:

Preserving authenticity is necessary at this site because the building was once a pilgrimage and leisure point for the entire area, so it is important to ensure that the conservation actions strengthen the spirit of the place and do not change the character of the building.

Encouraging public participation in planning and community involvement in determining uses in order to strengthen the connection between the community and the place and to restore its character as a community center that nourishes the community and is nourished by it.

An approach to conservation that combines sustainable planning to preserve the green and pleasant character of the place, such as advanced drainage solutions, conservation of vegetation, and installation of solar systems.

Recommended functions:

An educational center that combines learning about the technology of flour milling in the past.

Preservation of the green areas in order to preserve the spirit of the place that prevailed there in the past and to allow for a calm and serene experience.

A cultural area that combines activities and elements of leisure and fun in order to illustrate the cultural and community experience that existed around the area and around flour mills in the periods in which they operated.

Since this is the western part of the Yarkon River, clear planning boundaries must be defined around the mill to preserve the sacred area that includes access routes, walking paths, lounging areas, and other points of interest. The local heritage and community values must be taken into account to ensure the use of the place while preserving its authenticity, in combination with education and acquaintance with the history of the place, both the technological aspect that represents the flour milling method and the social-community aspect.

properties.cultural_assessment_0:
The Seven Mills complex includes a series of water-powered mills for grinding flour that were built in the Ottoman period and expanded in the 19th century. The complex is located adjacent to the Yarkon River, which provides them with high landscape value. Their location near the river, on the banks of the Yarkon, creates a natural and pastoral scene in combination with the archaeological remains from the Roman and Ottoman periods, which were built using local and advanced construction methods for that time, with the use of local stone and wood, reflecting the architectural character of their period.

The site has great historical value in the sense of being a testimony to the water technology and engineering methods that were in place during the Ottoman rule. The site reflects the influence of agricultural technologies on the local economy and serves as a key point for leisure activities along the Yarkon River. An in-depth investigation of the place reveals important archaeological finds linked to the Ottoman period and an understanding of how a structure designed for grinding flour by water functions and its contribution to the growth of the surrounding economy.

The scientific value of the site lies in its potential for researching water technologies and engineering fields from ancient times. The findings attest to the methods and materials used for the design and construction of the mills in their time, and they can be compared to other technologies that were in use during this period and later, and in other regions and countries. The mills provide unique information about the water system and infrastructure of the period, including water distribution and maintenance methods, which can contribute to a deeper understanding of the agricultural and rural way of life in those times.

The site has a high social value because it tells a story about an agricultural culture in the Yarkon River area and reflects how the business of flour milling can economically, culturally, and socially leverage villages. The site is one of the key points for the establishment of recreation and leisure areas along the Yarkon River because on many occasions there was a long queue for the milling buildings and there was a need for pleasant places to stay while waiting in line. The mills were centers for various activities such as grain milling, which created interaction between residents and different communities and contributed to community life and local trade. The site can leverage this story and transfer the experience to today's tourism and even try to restore it for our time as an educational and cultural recreation center.

properties.description:
The river is the second largest in the State of Israel and is characterized by a particularly strong water flow. This feature led to the establishment of flour mills on the banks of the river that used the power of the water flow for the flour milling operation. A total of 5 flour milling complexes were established along the Yarkon River, and we are focusing on the westernmost and largest complex, which included 11 milling facilities. The mill was established in a strategic location, which in the past allowed easy access to water sources and for transporting flour. The Yarkon River served the local population, and the water was identified as a critical resource for agriculture.

Archaeological findings discovered at the site in the 1990s indicate the construction of a bridge and a dam during the Roman period, which diverted the flow of the Yarkon River to a reservoir that was later used to operate the mills themselves. During the Crusader period, the area remained an important agricultural center.

The mill itself began operating in the Ottoman period and was an important part of the economic and social fabric of the area. Its mechanism was based, as mentioned, on diverting the flow of water from the Yarkon River to a reservoir. The water was divided into channels that led to the milling facilities, and each channel was used to drive one of the facilities. The water flowed through water wheels, which caused the grinding stones to rotate and grind the flour. After the process was completed, the water was channeled back to the Yarkon estuary.

The village of Jarisha (a name for a type of grain or grinding/milling in Arabic), which was located south of the Yarkon River, was an important flour milling center and is first mentioned in the 13th century. In 1596, it is mentioned that about 120 people lived in the village, and by 1931 the number grew to 183, and by the establishment of the state it reached 190. The village was located in a flat and agricultural area, which allowed its residents to engage in agriculture and develop advanced irrigation systems. It was home to a community based on agriculture, growing grains, vegetables, and fruits, with the flour mills also playing a central role in the local economy. The flour mills were used not only for grinding agricultural produce but also as a community gathering place. The mill itself was also operated by the villagers, and the mill manager was named Burkan.

Near Jarisha is also Tel Gerisa, a rich archaeological site that displays layers of human settlement from ancient times. The mound indicates active life in the area for hundreds of years and is a testament to the cultural and historical heritage of the entire region. Researchers believe that the mound was an important trade center, and the economic and social ties with the village of Jarisha allowed its residents to enjoy developed infrastructure.

During the British Mandate, the site was a major source of flour milling and provided 4,000 tons of flour per year, which fed 3,000 people. The mill also became a recreational center. Farmers came from afar and had to wait for their turn to grind their sacks of flour, so coffee shops and restaurants were established nearby, and after a few years, the place became a social center. In later stages, a boat dock was established nearby, which indicates a lot of activity at the mill site. In fact, it can be understood that the flour mills on the banks of the Yarkon were a key point for recreation and leisure on the banks of the Yarkon and shaped the cultural character of the river over the years and attracted tourists to the area.

During Napoleon's campaign in the Land of Israel, the place did not serve as a significant center, but the political and social effects of the campaign were evident on it. During World War I, the effects of the war caused interruptions in agricultural and business activity in the area, but the mill continued to maintain its economic importance.

During the Arab Revolt in the 1930s, tensions in the area affected the local economy, which led to a decline in the mill's activity. In 1936, the mill was closed due to the invention of steam and diesel technologies.

From 1936 to 1990, when the State of Israel was established, the place stood abandoned. Starting in the 1990s and early 2000s, efforts and excavations were made to restore the buildings and the complex and bring them back to public consciousness, which connects visitors to the history of the area. In 2008, plans began at the initiative of the deputy director of the KKL Central Region, landscape architect Yehiel Cohen, with the planning of the Bader Architects landscape architecture firm, headed by Zvi Bader and Tamar Ben-Tovim.

There are remains of a bridge from the Roman period and remnants of the dam. The reservoir and its location are clearly visible. Archaeological surveys have revealed the foundations of the mill buildings, which include limestone and kurkar for the facades and the vaults of the channels. The excavations have uncovered water wheels, grinding stones, and mechanical components of the mill. Wood was also used for the construction of wheels, although it has survived less. The findings include agricultural tools and implements, and provide information about the working methods and technologies of the period, which are suitable for the local agricultural environment.

properties.risk_and_sensitivity_description:
There are several risks and sensitivities that can affect the condition and purpose of the building:

  • Urban development around the Yarkon River as a desirable real estate area for development could endanger the site and its surroundings.
  • Water and air pollution from the area, especially due to its proximity to the Yarkon River, could affect the use of the place.
  • Poor maintenance of the ancient materials and the existing condition could lead to the deterioration of the building and the site's elements.
  • The success of sites of this type depends on maintenance actions by the authorities and users; incorrect use and maintenance can cause neglect and damage to the site.

Conservation work done in relation to the risks:

  • Filling joints, renewing and treating cracks in the walls of the building and in the elements found at the site.
  • Removal of uncontrolled vegetation around the site that could cause damage to the building in the future.
  • Strengthening the foundations of the building to cope with ground movements.
  • Preserving the original materials and creating a supportive environment for their current condition.
  • Installation of drainage systems to improve drainage in the complex and prevent the accumulation of water around it.

properties.conservation_policy_and_recommendations:
We are referring to the conservation area from the points of the historic bridge that was destroyed and in its place there is a new connection with busy roads, up to the point where there is the meeting of the historic stream course with the current course of the Yarkon River. We chose these boundaries because they include all the components of the mill and the elements that were historically related to it, such as the adjacent bridge. In addition, it is important to show the historical course of the stream and how it passed through the mills and the dam on the site, which sheds another point of light on how the site existed and operated before it was destroyed in World War I. Therefore, the meeting point of the historical and current stream courses are included as part of the conservation site of the 10 Mills-Al-Hadar complex.
We believe that the conservation project and the archaeological operation carried out in the area provided a clue as to how the mills operated in the area and what their layout was, but we believe that what was done is not enough. The part that we were missing the most is the conservation file that was not approved and has many deficiencies and therefore is not official. We would recommend completing the deficiencies and creating a conservation file that consolidates all the relevant materials from the Israel Antiquities Authority, the Ganei Yehoshua Company, the many historical testimonies, and more. In addition, there are other parts of the complex that have not been excavated and are currently in the areas of the cities of Bnei Brak and Ramat Gan. We believe that there is great historical importance in excavating these findings in light of the lack of much physical information and the great destruction of the mills.

properties.cultural_assessment_0:
Values-
1. Historical Value - The flour mill is located on a significant historical axis where several formative events occurred that are relevant not only on a regional level, but also on a global level. The site reflects the historical processes along the Yarkon, as part of the settlement boom in the area during the Ottoman period (19th century), which is also linked to a concentration of large mills along it. At that time, the Yarkon was the first among the other water sources in the Land of Israel. The place served as a bridge over the Yarkon on one of the main roads in the Land of Israel. Among the historical events that took place there were Napoleon's conquest campaign in 1799, the visit of the German Emperor in 1898, and the decisive battles between the Turkish army and the British army in World War I.
The site also reflects the destruction of the mill in World War I, its abandonment during the Mandate period, and the abandonment of the landowners in 1948 (the conquest of Sheikh Munis), which caused the mill and its story to disappear from the radar. Over the years, the development of the area as part of the Yarkon Park led to the exposure of the mill and the revival of its historical story.

2. Age Value - Some experts claim that the mills were built as early as the Crusader period and some even estimate that they were built even earlier in the Roman period.

3. Rarity Value - The mill is the only one in the Land of Israel that operated on such a large scale, and it serves as a unique historical milestone where many events took place.

4. Technological Value - The largest mill on the Yarkon River and even in all of the Land of Israel. The mill included about 20 grinding mechanisms, which was a technological precedent at that time in terms of the scale of the complex itself.

5. Natural, Landscape, and Ecological Value - As part of the rehabilitation process, a large basin was created that includes islands for nesting birds and animals. In addition, landscape treatment was carried out, which included rehabilitating the vegetation and bringing back stream species that had disappeared from this part of the Yarkon.

6. Social Value - As part of the rehabilitation and conservation actions carried out in the complex, seating areas and digital aids telling its story were added. In addition, the development of paths connecting the site to the rest of the Yarkon trails and the Israel National Trail, the place attracts a variety of populations.

7. Value of Human-Nature Interaction - The site is an outstanding example of traditional human settlement, of the use of a natural stream channel. An example representing an ancient culture of flour milling and grinding.

8. Economic Value - The mill is part of a tourist route operated by the Tel Aviv Municipality as part of guided tours through the flour mills and other conservation complexes along the stream.

Criteria: Value of Completeness and Authenticity - Today, at the site, parts of the flour mill located in the area of the Tel Aviv Municipality have been exposed after archaeological excavations and many conservation processes. The ancient dam is also not complete and is currently in a partial state. Many wings of the historical flour mill are not visible, and are located in the areas of the cities of Ramat Gan and Bnei Brak, which are planned to be exposed in the future. There is little physical evidence of the mills. The authenticity of the flour mills has been preserved; no parts that were exposed from the original site have been moved. No building additions have been added to the site, except for the construction of a monument near the archaeological site that symbolizes the ancient flour mills.

In conclusion, the detailed historical description attests to the effort to document and preserve the place, which has already interested archaeologists in the last century. The evidence from a variety of sources and periods in history, together with the writing about the site, attest to the desire to preserve information about the site and its consistent importance throughout history. The site was significant and important not only on a local level but also in global terms, such as the front in World War I.

properties.spirit_of_place:
We believe that the conservation of the site had historical but also social significance. From a tour of the site and collecting testimonies from the field, we saw how life was breathed into a historical site of all-regional importance, which became an active and attractive complex. As part of the lack of physical evidence, there is also still a lot to discover about the story of the mills.
Today, when we toured the site, we watched people learning about the mills using visual and digital means, sitting at their feet, and enjoying the view. Therefore, we find importance in the contemporary use of the complex. The mills are part of a wide system that began in ancient times when the Yarkon served as a natural resource that provided life along it and continues in our days to provide a variety of activities.
properties.description:
Yarkon Park is considered one of the most prestigious parks in Israel and serves as a center for recreation, sports, and leisure. The Yarkon River provided a strong water flow, which allowed the use of water power for grinding grains. It was available throughout the year, regardless of a specific season, was close to agricultural fields, and the type of soil in the area was suitable for the stable construction of the many mills along it. The flour mills served the local residents (Jews and Arabs) and the farmers in the area, who supplied the grains for milling.
'Ten Mills' is a site that included flour mills and a stone bridge. Some experts claim that the mills were built as early as the Crusader period and some even estimate that they were built even earlier in the Roman period.
The flour mill is located on a significant historical axis where several formative events occurred that are relevant not only on a regional level, but also on a global level, such as World War I in which the Ottomans fought with the British, the Jaffa-Nablus road on which Napoleon's army passed, and the defeat of the New Zealand cavalrymen. The mill is the only one in the Land of Israel that operated on such a large scale - it is considered the largest flour milling site on the Yarkon and thus constitutes a technological precedent. At its peak, twenty pairs of millstones operated there, but it got its name later when only ten pairs remained in operation.
It served as an important resource for the residents of the area at that time, Jews and Arabs who lived nearby, in the village of Sheikh Munis.

Components of the Mill:
A chute-type flour mill. The Yarkon water is dammed and passes through vaults from the front of the mill through sloped feeding channels in the form of a 'chute'. The water slides from the east into the mill and turns the paddle wheel and then returns to the river from the western front of the mill. A vertical axis connecting the paddle wheel to the millstones turns the upper millstone (the runner) which grinds the wheat grains placed on the lower stone (the bedstone). Apparently, 20 pairs of millstones operated at the site, providing about 30-40 kg of wheat per pair.

The Mill Through the Ages - A Historical Timeline:
1. 1099 - Stone Bridge - At the site of the mills on the Yarkon River, there was a stone bridge, Jisr al-Hadar, which created a kind of artificial waterfall that operated the flour mills. The bridge was the only one for hundreds of years and some believe it was there since the Crusader days.
2. March 14, 1799 - Napoleon's army marched over this bridge on its way from Jaffa to Acre. In addition, Jacotin, who served as a commander in Napoleon's army, documented and drew historical maps along the journey.
3. German Emperor - On October 26, 1898, the royal entourage of Wilhelm II (Emperor of Germany and King of Prussia) also passed over the bridge on its way from Haifa to Jaffa.
4. WWI 1917 - To the north of the Yarkon was the Ottoman army and opposite it was the British army. As part of the fighting in the area, the Turks blew up the bridge in order to cut off transportation routes, and the mills ceased to work. On November 24, the New Zealand Brigade and British infantry crossed the Yarkon and took control of Sheikh Munis, and retreated the next day.
5. 1993 Initial excavations at the site - The Israel Antiquities Authority conducted rescue excavations at the site every few years. A large rescue excavation took place in 1993 and a more in-depth excavation in 2005. Among other things, remains of the dam and the historic bridge, pottery, and coins from several historical periods were uncovered.
6. 2005 - In-depth excavation at the site - In 2005, the Israel Antiquities Authority continued to carry out excavations in the area, and after that, renovation and expansion work was carried out in the park, bicycle paths, ornamental plants, the old bridge that passed over the dam was removed and a new bridge was built.

Testimonies-

18th Century - Sheikh Munis-
Sheikh Munis was an Arab village, a quarter of whose residents were Jews. It was established in the Ottoman period, probably during the 18th century, and during the British Mandate period, the village expanded. The mills were operated by a partnership of two families – the Bidas family, who owned land in Sheikh Munis, and the Amuriya family, who owned land in Herzliya. The village was located on the coastal plain, about 3 km northeast of the Yarkon River estuary. In March 1948, the residents fled the village and its lands were annexed to the municipal area of Tel Aviv.

1839 Travel Journal-
On June 23, 1839, Sir Moses Montefiore and his wife, Judith, crossed the Yarkon on this bridge, and she wrote in her diary:
'We got up early today [in Jaffa] before the sixth hour... and within an hour we came to a stone bridge that was almost destroyed. And when we had crossed the Patras River we came at the ninth hour to the tomb of Allah ibn Alim.'

WWI Shell in the Mill Wall-
An earthwork contractor who was working on paving a path near the Ten Mills complex identified an unidentified object while working and pulled it out of the ground. He approached the Ganei Yehoshua workers to find out what he had pulled out of the ground, and they called the police and helped to keep passers-by away until the forces arrived. It then became clear that it was an old shell that had been buried for many years. At first, it was estimated that the shell was there from the Six-Day War, but later experts testified that the shell was a British artillery shell, fired during the campaign of the British and New Zealanders against the Ottoman army.

Early 1930s: Historical Documentation-
Ten Mills and the Yarkon River. A photograph from the early 1930s. Today, a section of the Israel National Trail crosses the historic site. A man and a woman can be seen leading their donkeys and crossing the stream.

Archaeological Report from 1941-
This document, written by the archaeologist Jones on March 19, 1941, is a report describing the remains of an ancient complex called Al-Hadar in the Jaffa sub-district. He was accompanied by Gill, who was the district engineer from the P.W.D. (Public Works Department). The site, located along the Yarkon River, consists of a partially broken dam, a well-preserved wall with arched openings, and the ruins of three flour mills. According to estimates in the report, the construction dates back to the Crusader and even the Roman period. According to the property owner, Said Bidas: 'The mills were restored by his ancestors in ancient times and remained active until their destruction by the retreating Turkish forces in 1917.'
The document provides detailed measurements and descriptions of the structures, noting changes in the structure, the course of the river over time, and how these affected the operation of the mills. It serves as an official record of the site's condition and historical significance as of 1941, and provides valuable information for future researchers and conservationists.

1941 Sandrec and Historical Maps-
Sandrec Jones, a Briton from the Antiquities Department, leaves a documented sketch with a lot of information in 1941. Most of the surviving structure is still exposed, but we see in the sketch the western dam to the south. The only mistake is that he describes the marked area as a mill, but it is an overflow channel that allows for lowering the water level upstream for maintenance by opening the gates.
In addition to Sandrec's testimony, a map from 1940 shows Sandrec's sketch more accurately. The water channels and the mill building are drawn.

1870s PEF Map-
A British map from the 1870s. The Palestine Exploration Fund map was prepared with the aim of locating and documenting all the places mentioned in the Bible and in rabbinic literature. The map includes areas surveyed throughout the Land of Israel west of the Jordan River, from the Upper Galilee region to Beersheba. The map was first published in 1880. On the map, in the area of the 10 mills, the word 'bridge' can be seen, where the road crossing the Yarkon was marked, where the British army and the Ottoman army fought. The proximity of the village of Sheikh Munis, from which the Bidas family who controlled the mills came, can also be seen.

Reasons for Conservation-

In World War I, 1918, the Turks blew up the bridge to prevent the British army from crossing the Yarkon, which caused the site to sink over the years until it was completely covered with vegetation and alluvium. The purpose of the conservation is to expose the historical and cultural asset to future generations.

The initial exposure of the findings was done by the Israel Antiquities Authority. The conservation of the entire site was done on behalf of the Tel Aviv Municipality through the Ganei Yehoshua Company and with the assistance of the Fund for Open Spaces. The planning and execution team includes the project manager Kobi Butbul, Arch. Tamar Ben-Tovim, landscape architect Aura Raphael, ecologist Liav Shalem, and expert in the reconstruction of ancient technologies Yeshu Drey. The work was done in coordination with the Israel Antiquities Authority, the Yarkon River Authority, and the Yarkon River Drainage Authority.

Changes in the Yarkon River course during the conservation process and exposure of the mills-

The beginning of the conservation work dealt with creating an alternative channel for the river, in order to dry up the natural river channel around the mills and remove all the enormous alluvium that had accumulated over the past decades. After drying the natural channel, the intervention of a tractor-like work vehicle was made possible, which within a few hours exposed the entire site.

In conclusion, the rehabilitation thus included returning the course of the river to its channel, creating a wide river basin that includes islands for nesting birds and animals, developing paths and seating areas, rehabilitating the vegetation, and bringing back river species that had disappeared from this part of the Yarkon.

All this alongside the exposure of the dam and the flour mill located in the northern part of the site. As part of the conservation process, the Tel Aviv Municipality and the Ganei Yehoshua Company erected a monument named 'Ten Mills' near the place a few years ago, near the archaeological remains.
